And because of that, even though
articles._body: Petroleum-based adhesives are everywhere: bonding the wood and drywall in a construction project, holding together the joints of furniture, and even sticking labels to otherwise recyclable containers. “The labels on a container are held up with petroleum-based glue. And because of that, even though you’re putting the container in the recycle bin, it will not get recycled,” says Patty Ferreira, MBA ’97, CEO and cofounder of Silvis Materials, which is combating this problem with its fully biodegradable cellulose adhesives.  When Ferreira began thinking about bio-based adhesives, in 2014, she started by modifying cellulose’s existing role as a stabilizer in adhesive emulsions and replicating the known adhesive properties of more expensive nanocellulose. Today, the formula can make adhesives from virtually every type of plant cellulose, and the MIT Startup Exchange (STEX) is helping Silvis work with packaging and construction companies to test the results. She expects the adhesive to cut production emissions by up to 80% and use half the energy of fossil-based glues. Read more at www.technologyreview.com/alumni-profiles .

articles.title: YouTuber finds niche as college admissions mentor
articles.summary: As a first-generation student from a small town, Gohar Khan ’21 had to navigate the college admissions process largely on his own. He founded his YouTube channel, Gohar’s Guide, to make things easier for other young people. Today, more than 10 million people follow Khan on social media for college a
articles._body: As a first-generation student from a small town, Gohar Khan ’21 had to navigate the college admissions process largely on his own. He founded his YouTube channel, Gohar’s Guide, to make things easier for other young people. Today, more than 10 million people follow Khan on social media for college application advice, study tips, and life hacks. He is also the CEO and cofounder of Next Admit, a consulting business that provides help with college essays, applications, and test preparation. “I’m on a mission to help students worldwide succeed inside and outside of school,” he says. Born in Pakistan, Khan moved to the United States when he was six months old and grew up in Connecticut, attending a public high school that rarely sent students to top colleges. “That, coupled with the fact that my parents hadn’t gone through the process themselves, made [applying to colleges] a little bit difficult,” he says. “I wanted to demystify the admissions process for a lot of people in the position I was once in.” Read more at www.technologyreview.com/alumni-profiles .

articles.title: Launching youth entrepreneurship
articles.summary: Even as a teenager, Laurie Stach ’06 says, she had a “crazy ambition to take on the world and solve problems.” At MIT, she realized she wasn’t the only one. “Adults always see these youth who are good at math and science and say, ‘You’re going to do great things—someday,’” says Stach. “Meanwhile, tr
articles._body: Even as a teenager, Laurie Stach ’06 says, she had a “crazy ambition to take on the world and solve problems.” At MIT, she realized she wasn’t the only one. “Adults always see these youth who are good at math and science and say, ‘You’re going to do great things—someday,’” says Stach. “Meanwhile, traditional education isn’t preparing them.” That’s why in 2012 Stach founded LaunchX, a for-profit entrepreneurship program that helps high school students build practical skills through an intensive summer program in which they start real companies. Stach says that students form teams, identify a problem, and build an actual product or service that they then take to market—often generating preorders or even revenue before the four-week program ends. Raised in Texas and the Carolinas, Stach majored in mechanical engineering at MIT and earned her MBA from Harvard Business School in 2011. She ran her first summer program on MIT’s campus with 30 students in 2013 and says “it kind of snowballed.” LaunchX now serves about 500 students per year across both in-person and online programs . Read more at www.technologyreview.com/alumni-profiles .

articles.title: A new stamp on cyberfraud prevention
articles.summary: For Rupert Young ’95, SM ’95, his career in data science and cybersecurity began when his grandfather gifted him thousands of stamps: He built intricate databases to catalogue them, displaying the “precise eye” for detail and nuance that his MIT application essay said would make him a good engineer.
articles._body: For Rupert Young ’95, SM ’95, his career in data science and cybersecurity began when his grandfather gifted him thousands of stamps: He built intricate databases to catalogue them, displaying the “precise eye” for detail and nuance that his MIT application essay said would make him a good engineer. Young is now chief product officer of ­MaxMind, whose work with IP-address location data and fraud prevention has made it a go-to resource. Streaming companies, security vendors, merchants, and ad-network providers use its signature tool, GeoIP, to determine how and where users are accessing services. This information makes it possible to ensure retail sites are using the correct currency, flag suspicious bank logins, and more. Young’s passion for engineering was shaped by internships, and he has paid it forward by volunteering at his children’s California high school and trying to keep up with what “the next generation of engineers are tinkering with.” The next generation of product innovation at MaxMind excites him too. “Working with my team to try to find patterns in data and solve challenging problems—to me, there’s no greater joy,” he says. Read more at www.technologyreview.com/alumni-profiles .

articles.title: AgeLab research inspires an A I startup
articles.summary: When Don Yansen ’63 arrived at the MIT AgeLab for a study on technology in care­giving for older adults, he didn’t plan to launch another company. But when he heard participants talk about how hard modern devices can be to use, he decided to develop an alternative. Yansen, a serial entrepreneur who
articles._body: When Don Yansen ’63 arrived at the MIT AgeLab for a study on technology in care­giving for older adults, he didn’t plan to launch another company. But when he heard participants talk about how hard modern devices can be to use, he decided to develop an alternative. Yansen, a serial entrepreneur who retired to care for his wife, earned an MIT degree in electrical engineering and a master’s in physics from Northeastern. “What I took from MIT was a good education and the feeling I could solve difficult problems,” he says. One such problem: Many older adults “can’t even use a modern cell phone,” he says, “and very few people can use something like an Apple Watch.” So Kiwi Health, which he founded in October 2024, sells a wristband controlled primarily by voice. Wearers can set reminders, make calls, send texts, and share health data, all without navigating screens. AI helps interpret these commands, accounting for the way voices may change with age. The device also measures health metrics and automatically alerts caregivers to falls.  Yansen’s hope, he says, is that it can “help seniors live the best life that they can.” Read more at www.technologyreview.com/alumni-profiles .

articles.title: Amping up T cells to target cancer
articles.summary: Vaccines that turn the body’s immune system against tumors have shown promise in clinical trials, and a handful have been FDA approved for certain cancers. In many patients, however, these vaccines don’t stimulate enough of a response, and the approach some researchers have taken to strengthening it
articles._body: Vaccines that turn the body’s immune system against tumors have shown promise in clinical trials, and a handful have been FDA approved for certain cancers. In many patients, however, these vaccines don’t stimulate enough of a response, and the approach some researchers have taken to strengthening it—delivering the vaccine along with immune-stimulating molecules called cytokines—can cause severe side effects. Now MIT chemical engineer Daniel Anderson and colleagues at MIT, Harvard, and the University of Houston have reported promising results with a different way of attacking the problem: amplifying the T-cell response to mRNA vaccines. The advance could lead to much more powerful cancer vaccines as well as stronger protection against infectious diseases. Most vaccines generate not only antibodies but also T cells that can activate antigen-­presenting cells, which help tell the immune system what to attack. In their study, the researchers boosted that response with a new type of vaccine adjuvant (a material that can help stimulate the immune system). It consists of mRNA molecules encoding two genes that can switch immune cells into a more active state by turning on certain signaling pathways.  In studies of mice modeling bladder cancer, colon carcinoma, melanoma, metastatic lung cancer, and more, injections of lipid nanoparticles containing the mRNA-­encoded adjuvant enabled the immune system to slow growth of some tumors and eradicate many others. This happened even when the mice were not given a vaccine against a specific cancer antigen, but when they were, the response was stronger still.  “When these adjuvant mRNAs are included in the vaccines, the number of antigen-targeted T cells is substantially increased. These T cells play an important role in the immune response,” Anderson says. The mRNA adjuvant also enhanced the immune response to immunotherapy drugs called checkpoint blockade inhibitors, which work by lifting a brake that tumor cells put on T cells and are FDA approved to treat several kinds of cancer.  “The microenvironment of solid tumors is often hostile to T cells and represents a major barrier to effective immunotherapy. We find that immune remodeling with these adjuvants creates a T-cell-permissive environment and promotes tumor rejection,” says Christopher Garris, an assistant professor at Harvard Medical School and one of the paper’s senior authors. The researchers also explored whether their adjuvant could boost the immune response to vaccination against viral infection. When they delivered the mRNA particles to mice along with covid or flu vaccines, they found that the vaccine generated a T-cell response 10 to 15 times stronger than usual. The researchers now plan to test this approach in additional animal models, in hopes of developing it for use in both cancer and infectious diseases.  Meanwhile, they are not the only MIT scientists making exciting advances with adjuvants. A group led by Ana Jaklenec, a principal investigator at the Koch Institute for Integrative Cancer Research, has used one to help the injectable form of the polio vaccine induce a strong mucosal immune response in the GI tract. That could help reduce viral shedding and transmission, a key objective of polio eradication efforts. But to date this immunity has been produced mainly by the oral form of the vaccine, and many countries have stopped using it because it carries rare risks that the injectable version does not.

articles.title: Taking your temperature from the inside
articles.summary: Oral and forehead thermometers may not accurately capture a person’s core body temperature, and the few ingestible temperature sensors on the market are so big they are hard to swallow and risk obstructing the GI tract. But MIT engineers created one that can send continuous temperature updates at a
articles._body: Oral and forehead thermometers may not accurately capture a person’s core body temperature, and the few ingestible temperature sensors on the market are so big they are hard to swallow and risk obstructing the GI tract. But MIT engineers created one that can send continuous temperature updates at a size of just six by four millimeters. To create it, the researchers built a circuit that can fit on a one-square-­millimeter silicon chip and designed an oscillator based on leakage current—the small current that flows through a circuit when it’s off. Its frequency varies depending on the temperature of the chip’s surroundings. The circuit detects temperature within 0.01 °C and can be powered with a 1.55-volt coin cell battery. A strategy known as backscattering further cuts energy consumption, allowing most of the power requirements to be outsourced to an antenna outside the body. It emits an ultra-high-frequency radio wave, which is modulated by an antenna within the sensor and sent back to the external one. By interpreting the changes in the radio wave, the external antenna can calculate the temperature value. The result is “the smallest ingestible capsule that we have seen for temperature-­sensing paradigms,” says Saransh Sharma, a former MIT postdoc now at the University of Cambridge, who is lead author of a paper on the work.  The researchers envision using it to monitor infection, observe patients during and after anesthesia, track fevers in children, help mark ovulation, and more. It could also be used to monitor athletes, soldiers, or anyone else exposed to extreme temperatures.  “A sensor like this gives us the ability to monitor infections and identify them early,” says Giovanni Traverso, an associate professor of mechanical engineering and one of the paper’s senior authors, along with MIT provost Anantha Chandrakasan. “That’s very relevant, particularly for at-risk populations like people who are immunosuppressed.” Ultimately, he hopes, it could replace other types of thermometers for everyone.

articles.title: Seeing through murky waters
articles.summary: When remotely operated vehicles settle on the seafloor or dig through a sand bed, they can kick up clouds of sediment that onboard cameras struggle to see through. Often, the only thing to do is wait until the dust settles. But a new system developed by Amy Phung, SM ’23, PhD ’26, and her advisor&#8
articles._body: When remotely operated vehicles settle on the seafloor or dig through a sand bed, they can kick up clouds of sediment that onboard cameras struggle to see through. Often, the only thing to do is wait until the dust settles. But a new system developed by Amy Phung, SM ’23, PhD ’26, and her advisor Richard Camilli, SM ’00, PhD ’03, of the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI), offers a solution.  In this technique, the vehicle first uses sonar to quickly map its surroundings. That technology doesn’t provide detailed resolution, but it works equally well in cloudy and clear water. And it allows a vehicle to safely get close enough to specific objects for cameras to visualize them more carefully. To speed up the processing so the mapping can be done in real time, the researchers combined the sonar tech with an image-­matching algorithm developed by researchers in France that quickly estimates the relative depth of each pixel in a 2D scene. “An analogy would be if you were to go into a china shop in the dark, and try to pick your way around to find a specific coffee mug without knocking things over,” Camilli says of their new technique. “This would allow you to do that.” He and Phung say applications could include scientific exploration, underwater construction and maintenance, and handling of unexploded undersea mines.

articles.title: Your brain on AI
articles.summary: Many people find AI-based chatbots helpful in keeping up with news, but a study by Pattie Maes and her colleagues at the MIT Media Lab points to a big problem with this strategy.  Participants who evaluated paired news headlines and images over the course of four weeks were initially 21% percen
articles._body: Many people find AI-based chatbots helpful in keeping up with news, but a study by Pattie Maes and her colleagues at the MIT Media Lab points to a big problem with this strategy.  Participants who evaluated paired news headlines and images over the course of four weeks were initially 21% percent more accurate at telling fake news from real when aided by a chatbot—but by week four, they’d become 15% worse at identifying fake news without AI than they were before (though roughly a quarter of them reported feeling better at it). The result reflects an “AI dependency paradox” that has been observed in other domains, including medicine.  “Users get excited about these ‘magical’ LLMs but forget that they’re just statistical models that predict the next ‘token’ in a sequence,” says Anku Rani, a PhD student in media arts and sciences and one of the lead authors of the study, along with fellow MAS PhD student Valdemar Danry, SM ’23.  The researchers also found, however, that certain AI styles were associated with stronger independent performance later on, even if they slowed people down at first. “AIs that ‘tell’ by providing direct answers are more likely to foster reliance, while those that ‘ask’ via Socratic questioning are better at engaging someone to actually learn how to discern the truth on their own,” says Danry. “But it’s very much a trade-off between speed and effort.”

articles.title: MIT tech powered the Artemis II livestreams
articles.summary: During the original US missions to the moon in the 1960s and ’70s, astronauts relied on radio-­frequency systems to communicate, sending grainy, low-quality images and videos to Earth. But on the Artemis II Orion mission in April, spacecraft transmitted crystal-clear footage at speeds on par with th
articles._body: During the original US missions to the moon in the 1960s and ’70s, astronauts relied on radio-­frequency systems to communicate, sending grainy, low-quality images and videos to Earth. But on the Artemis II Orion mission in April, spacecraft transmitted crystal-clear footage at speeds on par with those of home internet connections.  The livestreams so many people enjoyed were made possible through the Orion Artemis II Optical Communications System (O2O), developed by MIT Lincoln Laboratory in collaboration with NASA Goddard Space Flight Center. Based on infrared laser light, which can transmit 10 to 100 times more data per second than radio waves, the system downlinked nearly half a terabyte of data at up to 260 megabits per second. This data trove contained never-before-seen views of the basins and craters on the far side of the moon, a crescent Earth setting behind the moon, a nearly hour-long total solar eclipse, and flashes of light from tiny meteoroids striking the lunar surface. “Our goal was to demonstrate O2O’s operational utility for human spaceflight, extending the high-bandwidth connections that internet users enjoy on Earth to astronauts in deep space,” says lead systems engineer Farzana Khatri ’90, SM ’92, PhD ’96, a senior staff member in Lincoln Lab’s Optical and Quantum Communications Group.  “Participating in this historic mission … and having O2O be useful—I couldn’t have asked for anything more amazing in my career,” she says.

articles.title: World humanoid robot games show runners breaking records, bursting into flames
articles.summary: Record-breaking robot races are less substantial than household chore challenges.
articles._body: Viral videos of the World Humanoid Robot Games show sprinting robots beating the human 100-meter record held by Usain Bolt—but also feature running robots crashing into barriers and falling down because they cannot readily stop running. A few fallen robots even break at the waist in a shower of sparks or catch on fire. That demonstration of both robotic prowess and limitations came from the second edition of the World Humanoid Robot Games hosted in Beijing from August 22–26. Like the inaugural event held in 2025, this year’s event challenged humanoid robots to run fast, perform kung fu or dance moves, fight one another in kickboxing, and play soccer or table tennis. This year’s games also tested robots in more humdrum practical scenarios like washing and hanging laundry, where they appeared to lag behind typical human working speeds. That suggests the event organizers, including Chinese state media and the Beijing city government, are keen to showcase the commercial potential of humanoid robots at a time when China’s robotics industry is rapidly developing and testing such robots. articles.title: Is Bitcoin Out of Its Bear Market? These Analysts Think So
articles.summary: Bitcoin Magazine
articles._body: Bitcoin Magazine Is Bitcoin Out of Its Bear Market? These Analysts Think So Bitcoin is out of its bear market. But expect a possible pullback.  That’s according to analysts at crypto research firm CryptoQuant, who say the coin is behaving like it has done in the past. CryptoQuant founder, Ki Young Ju, wrote on X Tuesday that the asset had “entered into the early bull phase.” Ju Pointed to movements bitcoin made in its last cycle before entering a bull market, and said the coin was currently doing the same thing.  JUST IN: Bitcoin is currently having its 3rd best August EVER, currently up 25% this month pic.twitter.com/q45AHHpK4e — Bitcoin Magazine (@BitcoinMagazine) August 24, 2026 CryptoQuant research shows that bitcoin flows to derivative exchanges have started again, confirming that traders have entered “risk-on” mode, which “has marked the start of a new bull cycle” in the past.  And another analyst at the firm, Theophiluspep, wrote that while the coin was entering a bull market, “spot demand, ETF flows, and market momentum have turned decisively bullish, but elevated profit-taking, exchange inflows, and overbought conditions suggest a potential near-term cooldown.” He added: “This looks increasingly like a genuine regime shift into the early phase of a new bull market, driven more by improving spot demand and institutional ETF buying than by excessive leverage.” Bitcoin started surging last week. It is currently up 22% over a seven-day period and was recently priced at $78,716. It briefly touched $81,160 on Monday. Its rise comes after a sluggish June and July when it mostly traded below $65,000.  U.S. investors last week reversed course and bought up shares in the bitcoin exchange-traded funds, which had their best week since October — the same time bitcoin notched its record of $126,080. Data from Farside Investors shows that the funds — managed by the likes of BlackRock, Fidelity, Grayscale, and Morgan Stanley — received $1.9 billion in new cash.  The change in sentiment comes after the Treasury Department’s announcement last week to at least double the size of its long-dated bond buybacks. Since the Treasury made the announcement, yields have gone down, while bitcoin and gold have shot up. The dollar last week was trading at a three-month low and on track for its worst week of August. Bitcoin, on the other hand, had its best week since 2023.  Positive regulatory news coming out of the White House also helped: President Donald Trump held a meeting with crypto executives earlier last week, and urged lawmakers to get the Clarity Act over the line.  This post Is Bitcoin Out of Its Bear Market? These Analysts Think So first appeared on Bitcoin Magazine and is written by Mathew Di Salvo .

articles.title: Dolly Parton’s Life in Photos: From Smoky Mountain Girl to Queen of Country Music
articles.summary: The iconic singer/songwriter and cultural icon died at the age of 80 on Aug. 25.
articles._body: Dolly Parton has lived a truly remarkable life, from growing up as one of 12 kids in a tiny house in the Smoky Mountains to becoming one of the most revered singers, songwriters, performers and philanthropists in the world. In honor of the legendary star — who died at the age of 80 on Tuesday (Aug. 25) in Nashville — Billboard is looking back at her incomparable life and career in photos. Born almost 30 years before the digital camera was invented, the earliest photographs of Parton capture her world-famous smile at a time when her singular voice was heard only by her family and the beautiful Appalachian nature surrounding her beloved home in Locust Ridge, Tennessee. That would soon change as she began traveling to Nashville to pursue a career in music, signing her first record deal in 1965 shortly after moving to Music City — where she also famously met her husband of nearly 60 years, the late Carl Dean. What followed was an unforgettable run of musical excellence, starting with debut album Hello, I’m Dolly — a project that propelled her to a spot on The Porter Wagoner Show , from which sprang her seven-year musical partnership with Porter Wagoner. After their professional split in 1974, Parton fortified her career as a soloist with enduring hits such as “I Will Always Love You,” “Jolene” and “9 to 5,” winning 10 Grammys and 22 entries on the Billboard Hot 100 in the process. Parton will also forever be remembered outside of music for everything from her signature look to her kindness, activism, generosity and industrialism, founding her flagship Dollywood amusement park in 1986 and her Imagination Library program in 1995. As the world grieves the loss of a great, check out Parton’s life in photos below.

articles.title: Stars’ glaring roster flaw that must be fixed ahead of 2026-27 NHL season
articles.summary: The Dallas Stars have consistently been one of the top teams in the Western Conference over the last seven years. The Stars fell well short of expectations last year after losing in the first round of the playoffs to the Minnesota Wild. Despite the disappointing 2025-26 campaign, players such as
articles._body: The Dallas Stars have consistently been one of the top teams in the Western Conference over the last seven years. The Stars fell well short of expectations last year after losing in the first round of the playoffs to the Minnesota Wild. Despite the disappointing 2025-26 campaign, players such as Matt Duchene still have faith this team can compete . The Stars did not make a ton of offseason moves. They brought back Jamie Benn on a one-year deal, bringing back the long-time captain on a one-year deal. Meanwhile, they also signed Kyle Burroughs to a one-year contract. He spent the 2025-26 campaign with the Ontario Reign of the AHL, and has played just 201 games in the NHL since being drafted in 2013. Meanwhile, the Stars also brought back Jason Robertson on a one-year deal worth $12 million. This was after there had been speculation of an upcoming trade for the restricted free agent. Still, bringing him back ate into cap space. It caused the team to let people walk, while also trading away some other parts. The Stars lost a lot at the blue line Sergei Belski-Imagn Images As part of attempting to stay under the salary cap while also retaining players, the team lost some playmakers. The Stars traded away Maverick Bourque and Ilya Lyubushkin to the Nashville Predators in exchange for draft picks. Bourque was a restricted free agent and a former first-round pick. He was coming off a stellar season. Bourque found the back of the net 20 times while adding 21 helpers. There was no way to re-sign him and keep other parts, so his rights were moved. While the move creates a hole in the middle six of the forward groups and in secondary scoring, it does not create the biggest hole. Lyubushkin being dealt could create a bigger issue. He was a physical presence on defense, playing on the right side. At 32-years old, he also gave a veteran presence to the team. While his ice time decreased and he was limited to just 53 games, he was a reliable second- or third-rotation player behind Miro Heiskanen on the right side of the defense. Losing Lyubushkin alone would not be a massive issue, and one that could be overcome, but it was not the only loss. Alexander Petrovic departed for the Florida Panthers in free agency. Like Lyubushkin, he played under 16 minutes per game and saw just 54 games of action. Also like Lyubushkin, he provided a reliable veteran presence on the right side of the ice. Heiskanen will still take the top rotational spot on the right side. He averaged 25:28 of ice time per game last year, one of the highest totals of his NHL career. With the losses of Lyubushkin and Petrovic, there is very little depth behind him for the other 34:32 of the game. There is little depth behind Heiskanen on the right side Nils Lundkvist is expected to take the second rotation spot on the right side for the Stars this year. While Lundkvist is a former first-round pick of the New York Rangers, he has yet to break out at the NHL ranks and has had trouble staying on the ice. He has never played more than 60 games in a season. The blueliner also has little experience on the penalty kill, which would put extra strain on Heiskanen. Meanwhile, Tyler Myers is expected to be the third-rotation, right-side defender. Myers was acquired from the Vancouver Canucks during the season last year. The Stars got him at a fairly low cost, and it does give the team a veteran presence on the third rotation. He could also take some reps on the penalty kill and pair on the second rotation if need be. Regardless, there has been a steady decline in his production. Both his hit rate and takeaway rate have declined over the last five seasons. Meanwhile, his expected goal differential when on the ice has continued to decrease. If the decline continues, or if the worst case happens and the 36-year-old bottoms out, the Stars defense will be in trouble. With the combination that the AHL club does not have many right-side defenders to replace one of the three right-side defenders if they go down, depth could be an issue for the Stars. They could also bring up Kyle Burroughs, who they signed in the offseason. Although a 31-year-old AHL call-up is not inspiring. The Stars could flex one of the left-side defenders over, but it still creates a much weaker unit overall. The Stars had a solid defense last season, and could again this year. Regardless, the lack of depth at that one defensive spot is a hole that needs to be addressed sooner rather than when it is an emergency. The post Stars’ glaring roster flaw that must be fixed ahead of 2026-27 NHL season appeared first on ClutchPoints .

articles.title: South Carolina basketball to host Chris Paul II, son of future Hall of Famer, for recruiting visit
articles.summary: Chris Paul II, the son of future Hall of Famer Chris Paul and a class of 2028 point guard, will be on campus at South Carolina soon.
articles._body: A future Hall of Famer’s son will be on campus at South Carolina soon. GamecockCentral’s Wes Mitchell has confirmed that class of 2028 Valley Village (CA) Campbell Hall School point guard Chris Paul II , son of recently retired NBA star Chris Paul, will take an unofficial visit to Columbia. 247Sports’ Dushawn London was the first to report the news, saying the visit will take place on Sept. 19. South Carolina football will host Mississippi State at Williams-Brice Stadium that day, meaning Paul will have an opportunity to see the Gamecock fanbase in action. Paul has not yet publicly announced an offer from South Carolina. However, he does have one power conference offer to his name already: Wake Forest, his father’s alma mater. Like the Gamecocks, other major programs have been involved, though, so more offers could come through in the not-too-distant future. Have a question for the GamecockCentral staff? Ask it now on The Insiders Forum. The elder Paul is now an assistant coach at Campbell Hall, where he will help lead his son’s varsity team this winter. Heading into his junior season, the younger Paul is coming into his own as a prospect. Following a strong EYBL season this summer, he has generated more recruiting interest than ever. In fact, all five of his Division-I offers have come since June. Listed at 6-0 and 160 pounds, he is built similarly to his father. Unsurprisingly, he plays a high-IQ brand of basketball. Paul has a knack for finding open teammates, can run an offense, and has enough ball-handling and quickness to be a threat as a driver. Paul does not yet hold an official recruiting ranking from Rivals. However, he is a three-star prospect and top-20 national point guard, according to 247Sports. What do you think? Join the discussion on The Insiders Forum.

articles.summary: Davante Adams is an inspiration to his coach, even though the Dallas Cowboys basically laughed about covering him in a joint practice. Furthermore, a Cowboys insider brought receipts to push back on a claim by a Rams insider about Davante Adams being uncoverable. Here’s the initial wording, accor
articles._body: Davante Adams is an inspiration to his coach , even though the Dallas Cowboys basically laughed about covering him in a joint practice. Furthermore, a Cowboys insider brought receipts to push back on a claim by a Rams insider about Davante Adams being uncoverable. Here’s the initial wording , according to Nate Atkins via a post by Underdog NFL. “Davante Adams was “virtually uncoverable” in joint practice against Cowboys and Saints, per @NateAtkins_” And then the rebuttal , according to a post on X by Joseph Hoyt. “As we reported at the time: it looked like a true joint practice with both the Rams offense and the Cowboys’ defense making plays, including this near INT by Shavon Revel against Davante Adams. So yeah, this is a stretch.” What fun. War of the insiders. Cowboys secondary will be tested in Week 1 It’s not like the Cowboys have to wait until Week 15 against the Rams to prove their point. They can get with it in Week 1 against the Giants, who are expected to have receiver Malik Nabers back on the field , according to Sports Illustrated. “Nabers is recovering from a torn ACL, but appears to be back on track for Week 1 after shedding his red no-contact jersey during Monday’s practice,” Josh Sanchez wrote. “Barring a setback, it appears Nabers will be on the field.” Head coach John Harbaugh hasn’t firmly committed to Nabers returning to face the Cowboys, according to ESPN. “I just don’t want to make any kinds of statements like that,” Harbaugh said. “I think it’s reasonable to assume that. Those are all kind of things you can assume based on watching the guy practice. But the only thing I know more than you guys know is what the doctors and trainers tell me as far as his rehab. And that is he’s doing well.” The Cowboys are eager to show off their new defense. They have a new coordinator in Christian Parker. And their revamped secondary has Caleb Downs, DaRon Bland, Cobie Durant, Jalen Thompson, and Malik Hooker in the expected starting lineup. articles.summary: GoldandBlack.com's Brian Neubert joins host Derek Schultz for an update on Purdue basketball, some football talk and more.
articles._body: GoldandBlack.com’s Brian Neubert joins host Derek Schultz for an update on Purdue basketball, some football talk and more. https://youtu.be/epcqqvPqAcM Audio only Purdue football coach Barry Odom wants to protect college football (excerpt from Dub Jellison’s Aug. 24 story) 5-star PG Reese Alston gives the latest with Louisville, Houston, Kentucky, Purdue & LSU5-star PG Reese Alston gives the latest with Louisville, Houston, Kentucky, Purdue & LSU Watch More Just when you thought you’d seen everything in college football, it shows you something new. Players who signed deals with NFL teams, participated in training camps and even preseason games are now eyeing returns to  college football . Tight end  Dae’Quan Wright , a class of 2022 prospect who played two years each at Virginia Tech and Ole Miss, was waived by the Cleveland Browns and is now planning to join LSU’s roster. Several other former college football standouts are looking to take the same path, with schools potentially bulking their rosters through the pro ranks. Will Purdue be involved with players who went the pro route, but are now exploring returns to college football? “We have talked about it. I look at the value of the game of college football, and I want to protect that. At some point, it ends for everybody. You know what I mean? You have the ability now that we’re searching NFL rosters for guys that may or may not make a team, and then that we’re going to allow them back to play the game-it’s mind-boggling to me,” Purdue coach  Barry Odom  said on Monday morning. “I want to protect college football. It’s been around a long time. You know, we’re doing a lot of really great things. I don’t know that this is the best for the sport of college football and the opportunities that are created for young people who are of college age,” said Odom.

articles.title: Packers’ 53-man roster prediction for 2026 NFL season
articles.summary: There is the good side of things for the Green Bay Packers with Jordan Love. But there is a major concern on the offensive line, and that could impact cut day. Here is the Packers’ 53-man roster prediction for the 2026 NFL season. Matt LaFleur’s Packers enter the season with Super Bowl dreams. Bu
articles._body: There is the good side of things for the Green Bay Packers with Jordan Love . But there is a major concern on the offensive line , and that could impact cut day. Here is the Packers’ 53-man roster prediction for the 2026 NFL season. Matt LaFleur’s Packers enter the season with Super Bowl dreams. But many things have to fall into place for that to happen. And one of the first steps is making the right decisions on which players to keep. Quarterback (2) Jordan Love, Tyrod Taylor No need to spend a lot of time here. Taylor has big shoes to fill in a backup role after the work done last year by Malik Willis. But Taylor is a proven veteran, exactly what the Packers need behind Love. And that means McCord won’t make the cut. However, there’s a good chance he sticks on the practice squad. Running back (3) Josh Jacobs, MarShawn Lloyd, Chris Brooks It’s also pretty clear cut here. Pierre Strong Jr. could make a case. But Lloyd has finally shown the explosiveness the Packers saw when they drafted him. But there’s still an injury concern , according to channel3000.com. “Yes, if I’m being honest,” Packers running backs coach Ben Sirmans said. “I think a lot of us were [thinking that way]. That’s what’s going through your head, especially in the beginning. I think that’s only natural. But now it’s to the point where I don’t know how many restrictions we’re giving him now. “We’re starting to feel a lot more confident that he’s going to be fine. But you still have to be cautious. As much as you want to just jump in and just keep feeding him and keep feeding him, I think that part of it is still a work in process.” The comfort zone will help the Packers still with the top three and not add Strong to the 53-man roster. Wide receiver (6) Christian Watson, Jayden Reed, Matthew Golden, Savion Williams, Bo Melton, Skyy Moore One thing of note: The Packers don’t have an NFL WR1 in this group. Watson is the placeholder, but let’s be real. He has played 11, 9, 15, and 10 games in his first four NFL seasons. His career high in yards is 620. WR1? No way. So that means Reed or Golden will need to step into that role. Or maybe all three become a committee WR1. That’s the Packer way, right? The question is, do the Packers keep six and cut J. Michael Sturdivant? Or is he No. 7? I think he’s out, along with Isaiah Neyor. The reason for six instead of seven is because the Packers need a third tight end. Tight end (3) Tucker Kraft, Josh Whyle, Drake Dabney Luke Musgrave will eventually return. But he’s on the PUP list, and Kraft is returning from an ACL. That’s why Dabney makes the cut. At least initially , according to ESPN. “Kraft looks like he’s healthy enough to be ready for Week 1 after last year’s torn ACL,” Rob Demovsky wrote. “But there’s not a lot of proven production behind him. Luke Musgrave will likely stay on the physically unable to perform list because of a neck injury. This is the No. 1 spot for general manager Brian Gutekunst to upgrade via trade or waivers. Gutekunst kept four tight ends on his initial 53 last year.” Offensive line (10) Jordan Morgan, Aaron Banks, Sean Rhyan, Zach Bako-Bewele, Anthony Belton, Jacob Monk, Jager Burton, John Williams, Darian Kinnard, Donovan Jennings Oh, that weak group. It has been ranked among the worst in the NFL. Good luck, Jordan Love. Hope you stay upright. A bad offensive line is very un-Packers-like. But there it is. And that’s why the call for 10 keepers is important. Bad depth is better than no depth. Still, if the Packers need help elsewhere, Jennings isn’t a lock by any means. Defensive line (6) Devonte Wyatt, Karl Brooks, Javon Hargrave, Warren Brinson, Chris McClellan, Jonathan Ford Size matters for the Packers, and they should be OK with these guys. Sticking with six means Nazir Stackhouse and Anthony Campbell don’t make the cut. The wild card is Ford, who has played his way onto the roster. The Packers scooped him up from the Bears late last season, and he’s rewarding them this year. Ford said returning to the team that drafted him in 2022 was a big deal , according to Sports Illustrated. “I felt honored,” Ford said this week. “When I left, to be honest, I didn’t think I was ever going to be back. The fact that I was able to come back and jump right in the mix and finish those games with this team, it was a wonderful thing for me to be with a team and organization that favors you and that feels good about you as a player. “I think that’s the main thing is having confidence and being with people that see you as a good player.” Edge rusher (5) Lukas Van Ness, Barryn Sorrell, Brenton Cox Jr., Collin Oliver, Dani Dennis-Sutton The Packers don’t have a strength here — until Micah Parsons returns. And that could be quite a few weeks into the season. Fourth-round pick Dani Dennis-Sutton gets the nod here because, well, the Packers spent a draft pick on him. Sutton shook off an injury and got back on the field this weekend. It wouldn’t hurt for him to claim that position with Nyjalik Kelly and others still shooting for it. Linebacker (5) Zaire Franklin, Edgerrin Cooper, Isaiah McDuffie, Ty’Ron Hopper, Nick Niemann There aren’t major questions here. However, it’s still possible for Kristian Welch to earn the final spot over Niemann. Cornerback (5) Keisean Nixon, Carrington Valentine, Brandon Cisse, Benjamin St-Juste, Domani Jackson What happens if the Packers decide not to start Nixon? Will that change how they mold this room in terms of the 53-man roster? Nixon has been viewed as being in competition to get a starting spot, according to ESPN. “I guess I’m being punished right now, I guess, I don’t know,” Nixon said Sunday. “I don’t really worry about what I’m running in camp, ones or twos. I just keep my process and just compete — for real.” If the Packers don’t do something and cut Nixon, this room should be solid. Could Kamal Hadden make the cut and

articles.title: What 49ers’ Kyle Shanahan, Fred Warner said about Jed York arrest
articles.summary: San Francisco 49ers owner Jed York has recently come under scrutiny due to his use of a pseudonym in response to a fictitious advertisement prior to his arrest at an Ohio trailer park. This incident has led to a plea agreement involving two misdemeanors and a two-day jail sentence. On Tuesday, th
articles._body: San Francisco 49ers owner Jed York has recently come under scrutiny due to his use of a pseudonym in response to a fictitious advertisement prior to his arrest at an Ohio trailer park. This incident has led to a plea agreement involving two misdemeanors and a two-day jail sentence. On Tuesday, the football leadership of the San Francisco 49ers addressed the controversy directly, presenting a united front that aims to shield the locker room from any off-field executive disturbances. According to The Athletic’s David Lombardi on X, head coach Kyle Shanahan emphasized that the franchise’s football operations function independently from front-office matters, effectively insulating players and coaches from non-football-related distractions. All-Pro linebacker Fred Warner echoed this sentiment, stating, “It really wasn’t a conversation being had in the locker room… It’s a personal situation.” As Lombardi noted on X, the clear operational divide between ownership and the regime led by Shanahan and general manager John Lynch, established in 2017, explains why no one inside the organization questioned whether York’s arrest would affect on-field performance. Shanahan elaborated on this dynamic , saying, “Jed’s entrusted the football operations to people who are involved in football, and players feel that. I’ve been in too many other buildings where issues do trickle down. Here, it’s pretty black-and-white. It’s always football decisions, because they know Jed has put us in charge of making those. It’s run from a complete football standpoint, and that’s what’s refreshing here.” This is a big-picture key to know: No one seriously questioned if Jed York's arrest would affect the 49ers on the field, and the separation York established between himself and Kyle Shanahan/John Lynch in 2017 is why. Shanahan: "Jed's entrusted the football to people who are… https://t.co/QMM4MeWM7o pic.twitter.com/bdZanxhfrH — David Lombardi (@LombardiHimself) August 25, 2026 Shanahan also acknowledged the personal weight of the situation, adding, “Obviously, it’s a very tough situation. It’s extremely fresh, a very personal situation. I have a lot of respect for Jed. I have a lot of respect for Danielle. Their family means a lot to me. With it being this personal, I’m trying my best to keep it that way.” In the aftermath of the legal proceedings, further details have emerged. Reports from TMZ indicate that York’s court fines were paid online under the name “D Cory,” which refers to Dan Cory, the CEO of Nickel Group, a prominent private security and risk management firm that protects 49ers executives and players. With the legal matter resolved and team leaders maintaining operational separation, the San Francisco 49ers are now focused on the upcoming regular season. articles.summary: New Louisville guard Seth Trimble, who recently transferred from North Carolina, has reportedly joined a Kentucky state lawsuit challenging the NCAA eligibility rules in an effort to secure a fifth season of collegiate eligibility, according to On3’s Joe Tipton and Cardinal Sports. Louisville
articles._body: New Louisville guard Seth Trimble , who recently transferred from North Carolina , has reportedly joined a Kentucky state lawsuit challenging the NCAA eligibility rules in an effort to secure a fifth season of collegiate eligibility, according to On3’s Joe Tipton and Cardinal Sports . Louisville previously announced Trimble’s transfer addition last week after the former UNC star recently committed to transfer following a Colorado court ruling that declared all Class of 2022 eligible to play the upcoming 2026-27 season in line with the NCAA’s new five-for-five age-based eligibility model. The Tenth Circuit of Appeals recently granted the NCAA’s request for a stay , effectively reversing the class-action ruling for all Class of 2022 recruits who do not otherwise have another temporary injunction. [ $19.99 gets you a FULL year of On3 | Rivals national coverage ] By joining the Kentucky eligibility suit, which was filed in Jefferson Circuit Court, Trimble is seeking such an injunction to facilitate his ability to play out the 2026-27 college basketball season at Louisville. The Kentucky state class-action suit includes fellow plaintiffs such as Cardinals defensive backs D’Angelo Hutchinson and Jabari Mack , as well as Kentucky basketball transfer Mark Mitchell , who was granted an injunction last Friday . Trimble’s addition to the Cardinals’ roster was seen as quite the offseason coup for third-year Louisville coach Pat Kelsey . “Seth Trimble is one of the steadying forces in college basketball,” Kelsey said in a statement released from the school, via Cardinal Sports . “There’s no question that he will have an immediate impact on what we have been building this offseason. Seth is a tenacious, physically imposing presence that makes his impact felt on both ends of the floor. He’s incredibly familiar with what it takes to compete at a high level in the ACC, and he brings it night in and night out. “He has a special blend of maturity, poise and leadership qualities that will endear him to Card Nation.  I firmly believe he’s the type of competitor and human that will flourish in our program. It was apparent from day one of recruiting him that Seth’s goals align with our vision, and we are thankful that he has decided to join us on this journey. The opportunity to sign such a high-quality player and person with this much experience at this point in the year is certainly unique, but we know Seth will fit right in with what we have here in Louisville.” Trimble, a 6-foot-3 guard who averaged 14.0 points, 3.8 rebounds and 3.0 assists across 24 games last season as a senior at UNC. This report will be updated.

articles.title: Week 0 is here: One reason to watch all eight games
articles.summary: Week 0 is here with eight games to kick off the 2026 college football season. Here’s one reason to watch every game on Saturday’s schedule.
articles._body: Kentucky Football still has a little longer to wait before the season opener in Lexington, but college football is back this weekend. The Wildcats won’t kick off the Will Stein era until Sept. 5 in Lexington. Before then, Week 0 gives us eight games this Saturday to scratch the college football itch, beginning overseas and continuing throughout the day back home. No, it’s not the full Saturday slate we’ve been waiting eight months to see. But it’s real college football, and that’s enough for us. So, in chronological order from the first kickoff to the late-night finish, here is one reason to watch each of the eight games kicking off the 2026 season. Bill and Jordon in Dublin One of the sport’s great traditions returns this weekend. The Aer Lingus Classic is back, with North Carolina and TCU kicking off Week 0 in Dublin’s Aviva Stadium. The Horned Frogs are a touchdown favorite against the Tar Heels in a rematch of Bill Belichick ‘s college coaching debut, when TCU spoiled Belichick’s launch with a 48-14 win in Chapel Hill last season. This year, Belichick has the help of Bobby Petrino , his new offensive coordinator in the UNC Football soap opera. USC is Week 0’s only ranked team Back in the States, NBC’s afternoon game features the only ranked team playing Week 0 football. No. 14 USC hosts San Jose State in a noon game at the Coliseum. The 38.5-point spread suggests a blowout in the Trojans’ 2026 home opener. Still, it’s a first look at Lincoln Riley ‘s fifth season at a program seeking a return to prominence and its first College Football Playoff appearance. Jayden Maiava is back as USC’s QB after a 3,711-yard season a year ago. The Trojans scored 73 points in this spot last season. Pretend the ACC game is in Brazil There’s one conference game in Week 0. The ACC couldn’t wait to show off its league, so two ACC teams will shake up the early standings with a head-to-head. Virginia and NC State were picked sixth and seventh in the league’s preseason poll, but one of them will claim first place by Saturday evening in Charlottesville. It’s NC State’s first ACC road game to open a season in 52 years. The game was originally scheduled to be played in Brazil, marking the first-ever college football game in South America. But those plans were scrapped in June, and the game was moved from Rio to Virginia’s Scott Stadium. That’s not as fun as an international game, but it’s the first game of the year with conference implications. North Dakota State’s first FBS game North Dakota State was a wagon in the FCS, winners of 10 national championships since 2011. Before that, ND State won five Division II championships, part of a trophy case that has 18 national championships in total with 39 various conference championships. With that success, the Bison are taking another step up in 2026, joining the big boys in the FBS in the Mountain West Conference. The first FBS game in school history is this Saturday in the Fargodome. The opponent? Jacksonville State, which made the FBS jump in 2023. Sacramento State’s first FBS game There’s football in Ypsilanti this weekend. Eastern Michigan opens its season Saturday night, hosting Sacramento State in The Factory. It’ll be the first time that EMU has ever hosted a California school, so that’s neat. Even neater, it’s Sacramento State’s first game in the FBS, as the Hornets join North Dakota State as the two new FBS schools in 2026. Stanford looking for Week 0 payback vs Hawaii Hawaii beat Stanford with a walk-off field goal in Week 0 last year, winning 23-20 in Honolulu. This year, Stanford hosts the Week 0 rematch, with first-time head coach Tavita Pritchard , a former Stanford quarterback and assistant coach, leading the Cardinal. Meanwhile, Hawaii has its former quarterback legend, Timmy Chang , back for his fifth season as head coach. Chang looks to take his alma mater another step forward after improving the team’s win percentage every year since he took over. Florida State begins its road back Coming off back-to-back losing seasons, Florida State enters the new year unranked and out of the conversation. The Seminoles are a 31.5-point favorite against New Mexico State on Saturday, so a win won’t lighten the pressure around Mike Norvell . But it’s worth tuning in, especially if the Aggies keep the score respectable in Tallahassee. Norvell has one of the hottest seats in the country and a new-look offense, so he needs to avoid a Week 0 sweat. Dan Mullen’s second act in Vegas UNLV is the Mountain West favorite, and the fourth Mountain West team playing this weekend. The Rebels will wrap up Saturday’s college football slate with the first game of the second year of Dan Mullen , hosting Memphis in the desert. Memphis was picked second in the American Conference’s preseason poll as the Tigers start a new era under Charles Huff . Neither team has committed to a quarterback, but the nightcap should be a high-scoring game with two teams excited about the future. The outcome could weigh into the Group of Six picture later in the year. articles.title: Bitcoin Breakout Could Be Around the Corner as Asset Is No Longer Oversold: Fairlead Strategies’ Katie Stockton
articles.summary: Bitcoin Magazine
articles._body: Bitcoin Magazine Bitcoin Breakout Could Be Around the Corner as Asset Is No Longer Oversold: Fairlead Strategies’ Katie Stockton Bitcoin is no longer oversold but there’s still time to buy, according to Fairlead Strategies’ Katie Stockton.  Speaking on Tuesday to CNBC, the financial research firm’s managing partner said that Bitcoin cleared its 200-day moving average back in May, meaning that a potential breakout could be coming.  Bitcoin started rallying last week on news that the Treasury would at least double the size of its liquidity-support buyback operations. It’s up over 22% over a seven-day period, and was recently trading for $78,915. The coin traded above $81,000 on Monday.  JUST IN: Fairlead Strategies founder tells CNBC Bitcoin is "not over bought yet, so that's the good thing." "We're looking for more upside from gold…maybe it won't be quite as long lived as what we expect from Bitcoin" pic.twitter.com/lXly8WRO3Y — Bitcoin Magazine (@BitcoinMagazine) August 25, 2026 “It’s not overbought yet, so that’s the good thing,” said Stockton.  “Whenever you see a breakout above a resistance level, it’s always better to have that immediate follow-through to essentially confirm the breakout.”  Bitcoin was trading under $65,000 for most of June and July and experiencing its lowest volatility in its 17-year history.  Its recent rally has some analysts saying that the so-called debasement trade could be hot again. The debasement trade is when investors buy assets when they think fiat money is losing value.  And losing value it is: The dollar slid following the Treasury’s announcement last week. Gold and bitcoin have since rallied.  Bitcoiners have long argued that the biggest cryptocurrency can work as a hedge against government printing, along with precious metals.  U.S. investors last week piled back into Bitcoin exchange-traded funds; the investment vehicles had their best week since October, with nearly $2 billion in inflows.  Bitcoin’s price was also helped after President Trump last week gathered with crypto executives at the White House and said that getting the Clarity Act over the line would keep the U.S. ahead of China.  Lawmakers were hoping to get a vote on the crypto market structure bill, or Clarity Act, in August. A vote will now go ahead in September. The bill will establish a framework for distinguishing between digital assets that are securities, commodities or payment stablecoins.  This post Bitcoin Breakout Could Be Around the Corner as Asset Is No Longer Oversold: Fairlead Strategies’ Katie Stockton first appeared on Bitcoin Magazine and is written by Mathew Di Salvo .

articles.title: ESPN debunks ‘completely false’ rumors about not renewing WWE contract
articles.summary: Despite rumors of ESPN and WWE’s PLE broadcast deal not being renewed upon expiration in a few years, that does not appear to be the case. ESPN responded to a report from SEScoops that alleged the network “won’t be renewing the [WWE PLE] contract when it expires,” calling it 
articles._body: Despite rumors of ESPN and WWE’s PLE broadcast deal not being renewed upon expiration in a few years, that does not appear to be the case. ESPN responded to a report from SEScoops that alleged the network “won’t be renewing the [WWE PLE] contract when it expires,” calling it “completely false,” via the Wrestling Observer. “There is no truth to the report that we have decided not to renew,” ESPN responded. “They never checked with us before publishing and had they, we would have told them that was completely false.” So, it sounds like there is no tension to speak of between the two sides. There are still about four years left on the deal. It remains to be seen if they will re-up it when the time comes. WWE and ESPN’s $1.6 billion PLE broadcasting deal Joe Camporeale-Imagn Images In 2025, WWE and ESPN signed a broadcast deal worth an estimated $1.6 billion. It took WWE PLEs from Peacock, where they had resided for years, and made them available to stream on ESPN Unlimited. The first anniversary of the deal is approaching. The first WWE PLE to broadcast on ESPN was Wrestlepalooza. The show was headlined by AJ Lee’s big return and John Cena vs. Brock Lesnar for the last time. ESPN Unlimited is about to increase its subscription prices , too. Monthly subscriptions are going from $29.99 to $31.99, and yearly subscriptions are going from $299.99/year to $319.99/year. That may not sound like a big difference, but that adds up to a $24 increase over a full year for the monthly plan and a $20 increase for the yearly plan. Coming up, WWE still has two more PLEs to air this year. Money in the Bank and Survivor Series: WarGames will take place on Oct 10 and Nov. 28, respectively. There is always a chance that Crown Jewel, which has been a yearly PLE every year since 2018 (except in 2020), is added to the schedule. Then, the Road to WrestleMania 43 begins with the Royal Rumble in February 2027. The post ESPN debunks ‘completely false’ rumors about not renewing WWE contract appeared first on ClutchPoints .

articles.title: Utah OL Going All in on Being Great Under Jordan Gross
articles.summary: Utah offensive line coach Jordan Gross says his room is going all in on being great for the 2026 season.
articles._body: The big guys up front remain one of the biggest talking points as Utah’s 2026 season inches closer. Strides have been made, according to first-year offensive line coach Jordan Gross , and the unit continues to be 10 deep despite no starters being named yet. “It’s been an outstanding fall camp. All the credit goes to our players on that offensive line. Everything from no returning starters to a new offense to a new O-line coach. There’s just so much that they’ve had to take on, and every day has been just even more encouragement to me that they are all in on being a really great unit this year,” Gross said on Monday. In the first week of fall camp, Gross said he felt comfortable with 10 players in his room, and he stuck to that number with just a little over a week until the start of the season. “Still working to identify who that first five will be when we take the field, and that’s a very good thing. Not, oh crap, who is it going to be? Like dang it, who do I need to pick out of this unit? So been a lot of fun. I’m very lucky. It’s a great group,” Gross said. A handful of members of the offensive line dealt with some minor injuries during fall camp, which allowed Gross to play with his lineups. “The beauty of that has been we’ve had a lot of different combinations when we’ve called that first group up. It’s been a different unit a number of times,” Gross said. “There are some guys that have more experience or are better than others, but that depth development has been the bright spot, even more so than our first five. That second five that we think we could win a game with is what’s really nice for us right now.” Roger Alderman , Isaiah Kema , Reece Parmenter, and Cedric Jefferson were all called out as guys who put themselves into the mix during fall camp. True freshman Kelvin Obot also continues to be in the mix, and that can be credited to his relationship with Gross. “I think it’s benefited Kelvin a lot that he didn’t have to switch to a different coaching style, different lingo, different way of doing things, different level of expectations. It’s been about as smooth of a transition as a person could ever get,” Gross said. “But what’s been really neat about my relationship with Kelvin has been that I get to coach him at a lot deeper level than I did before, when we were a small high school team, and we had five minutes for individual, and then we had to move on to something else. And so he’s a sponge for knowledge, and he’s an incredibly driven, hardworking young man, and it’s even become more apparent since we’ve been here together.” Watch the full press conference below: Gross also addressed the communication standard among his group and shared updates on other members of the OBLOCK in the video below: Take your Utah fandom to the next level by joining the ultimate community for dedicated fans at UteZone. articles.title: Big Ten punishment revealed for schools that violate new NFL rule
articles.summary: On Tuesday, the Big Ten officially passed a rule that bars players from returning to college football from the NFL to play for a Big Ten school. The ADs were unanimous in support. This rule comes on the heels of multiple lawsuits that have been passed, which have allowed players waived from training
articles._body: On Tuesday, the Big Ten officially passed a rule that bars players from returning to college football from the NFL to play for a Big Ten school. The ADs were unanimous in support . This rule comes on the heels of multiple lawsuits that have been passed, which have allowed players waived from training camp rosters to utilize a fifth year of college eligibility in 2026. Violating the new Big Ten-NFL rule will result in a coach suspension of 50% of contests and an institutional fine, On3’s Pete Nakos reported Tuesday afternoon. The punishment is similar to the one the NCAA has in place for “ghost transfers,” or players who leave one school for another without entering the transfer portal. $19.99 gets you a FULL year of On3 | Rivals national coverage “The Big Ten Conference announced Tuesday that unanimous adoption of a conference rule to prohibit football players who have signed a professional contract, were on a professional roster at any point or declared for the NFL Draft as an underclassman without withdrawing, from maintaining eligibility for athletic competition at a conference institution,” a statement from the conference read. “The conference continues to evaluate potential rules restricting professional athletes in other sports from conference competition.” Other conferences are reportedly considering similar rules to Big Ten The ACC and SEC are considering similar rules, per Nakos. The conferences, however, have yet to make a ruling. The SEC has already seen two such players that would be affected by these rules: former Ole Miss stars TE Dae’Quan Wright and DL Xzavian Harris . Harris was signed by the New Orleans Saints as an UDFA this offseason, and Wright appeared in multiple preseason games for the Cleveland Browns. They both, however, have already committed to play for Lane Kiffin and LSU this season. On Monday, the SEC  issued a statement  that said, “College athletes, not former professional athletes, have been at the heart of the Southeastern Conference. Individuals who choose to leave college athletics, sign professional playing contracts, and compete professionally should not then be permitted to return to college competition. “Allowing that to occur will blur the line between college and professional sports, create significant competitive equity concerns, and reduce opportunities for high school and current college athletes. College sports are for college athletes. The current confusion around national eligibility standards emphasizes the need to advance the Protect College Sports Act.” With this saga moving at light speed, it will be worth watching to see what steps other conferences take. After all, the 2026 college football season kicks off in just a few days with Week 0 coming up on Saturday.

articles.title: Buccaneers’ 53-man roster prediction for 2026 NFL season
articles.summary: The Tampa Bay Buccaneers are at a crossroads heading into the 2026 season. This may be QB Baker Mayfield’s last ride with the Buccaneers given his contract standoff with the team. That will put a lot of pressure on him, and the entire organization, to finally make a deep playoff run this ye
articles._body: The Tampa Bay Buccaneers are at a crossroads heading into the 2026 season. This may be QB Baker Mayfield’s last ride with the Buccaneers given his contract standoff with the team. That will put a lot of pressure on him, and the entire organization, to finally make a deep playoff run this year. The preseason is almost over, which means NFL teams around the league will soon need to make their final roster cuts. Tampa will be faced with some difficult decisions to assemble their best group of 53 players. Which players will make the final cut and represent the Buccaneers during the 2026 season? Here is one version of what Tampa’s 53-man final roster could look like entering the regular season. Quarterbacks (2) Baker Mayfield, Jake Browning Some fans may be surprised to see that only two quarterbacks make the final roster. Mayfield is entering what could be his final season in Tampa Bay. The Buccaneers will be heavily relying on him to have a big season. If Mayfield does get hurt, Browning will be the team’s next best option. Remember, the NFL’s Emergency Third-Quarterback Rule allows teams to dress a third QB on game days without using a normal roster slot for him. In this scenario, the Buccaneers will make full use of this rule. They will likely keep Jalon Daniels on the practice squad for such a situation. Running backs (3) Bucky Irving, Kenny Gainwell, Sean Tucker It could make sense to keep four running backs, but the Buccaneers opt for a trim depth chart at the position. That decision will allow them to add more depth at other positions. Irving enters his third season as Tampa’s starter with big expectations. Hopefully he can stay healthy after last year’s injury-plagued season. Meanwhile, Gainwell will take over the Rachaad White role and Tucker should reprise his usual duties. If the Buccaneers do need to add more depth, they can simply elevate someone from the practice squad. Or grab a veteran free agent. Wide receivers (6) Chris Godwin Jr., Emeka Egbuka, Jalen McMillan, Tez Johnson, Ted Hurst III, Kameron Johnson No big surprises here. Godwin and Egbuka are two excellent targets for Mayfield. But depth at wide receiver is one of Tampa’s most underrated strengths. Both McMillan and Johnson have flashed potential during the NFL careers. Hurst should fit right into that group, as he’s looked good during training camp . Tampa can do a little bit of everything with all of these receivers. Meanwhile, Johnson keeps his roster spot as a return specialist. Tight ends (3) Cade Otton, Payne Durham, Ko Kieft In this scenario, the Buccaneers decide to cut both Bauer Sharp and Devin Culp at the roster deadline. Both players have a shot at making the final roster, but keeping extra tight ends takes away roster spots at other positions. Tampa would likely bring at least one of them back on the practice squad, if not both. Offensive linemen (9) Tristan Wirfs, Ben Bredeson, Graham Barton, Cody Mauch, Luke Godeke, Benjamin Chukwuma, Justin Skule, Dan Feeney, Billy Schrauth No big surprises on the offensive line either. Tampa has an excellent group of starters and solid depth at every position. Upgrades could be coming in the future, but Tampa should be fine with this group for the 2026 season. If the Buccaneers did keep a 10th offensive lineman, it would likely be Ben Scott. Defensive linemen (6) Vita Vea, Calijah Kancey, A’Shawn Robinson, Elijah Roberts, Rakeem Nunez-Roches, DeMonte Capehart The Buccaneers look solid on the defensive interior, especially now that Vea is happy with his new contract . Tampa has enough talent to do line shifts on the interior if they wanted to. Their incredible depth should bring some consistency to the defense and limit huge runs up the middle. Edge rushers (6) Rueben Bain Jr., Yaya Diaby, Al-Quadin Muhammad, Anthony Nelson, David Walker, Mohamed Kamara Tampa has slowly been building an excellent group of edge rushers. That group now looks talented at the top and deep behind the starters. Bain should change the entire complexion of Tampa’s defense. The talented rookie is a monster both defending the run and getting after the passer. If he can adapt to the NFL quickly, he could be a force multiplier for the Buccaneers on defense. Meanwhile, the combination of Diaby, Muhammad, and Nelson gives Tampa plenty of options on the edges. And if they want to get creative, they can always kick Bain or Muhammad inside and lean on their reserve players in Walker and Kamara. Former second-round pick Chris Braswell is the most surprising roster cut in this scenario. Linebackers (4) Alex Anzalone, Josiah Trotter, SirVocea Dennis, Christian Rozeboom Tampa is throwing all of their chips behind newcomers Anzalone and Trotter, their projected starters in Week 1. Meanwhile, Dennis and Rozeboom should serve as high-level depth pieces and special teams contributors. None of the Buccaneers’ other depth players at the position received any consideration here. Both due to their talent level and because there simply isn’t any additional room left on the 53-man roster. Cornerbacks (6) Zyon McCollum, Benjamin Morrison, Jacob Parrish, Keionte Scott, Damarion Williams, Ayden Garnes Tampa decides to keep six cornerbacks here, and for good reason. Morrison is dealing with a hamstring injury , which makes his availability an open question before the regular season. Fortunately, McCollum and Parrish are solid all-around starters. Plus the Buccaneers added Scott in the draft, who can play almost any position in the secondary. He should get on the field quickly during his rookie season, even if just in a reserve capacity. The Buccaneers opt to keep Garnes over Josh Hayes here. Hayes is a great special teams contributor, but that depth can come from other positions like safety and wide receiver. articles._body: The Chicago Bears suffered an injury scare involving offensive tackle Darnell Wright during Tuesday’s practice as the team prepares to close out its preseason against the Tennessee Titans on Saturday at 6 p.m. ET on NFL Network. Wright exited red-zone drills after participating in just two plays, raising questions about his availability with the 2026 regular season approaching. ESPN’s Courtney Cronin reported Tuesday via X, formerly known as Twitter. “Darnell Wright came out of red zone drills after 2 plays and was replaced by Theo Benedet at right tackle. He’s now headed back into the building.” The Bears have yet to announce the severity of Wright’s apparent injury or a potential timetable for his return. Wright has developed into an important piece of Chicago’s offensive line since the Bears selected him with the No. 10 overall pick in the 2023 NFL Draft. Any extended absence would create another concern for the offense heading into the regular season. Chicago enters its preseason finale looking to bounce back from a 27-9 loss to the Cincinnati Bengals on Saturday . Following the matchup with Tennessee, the Bears will turn their attention toward Week 1. articles.title: How Did KATSEYE’s ‘WILD’ Manage Such a Record-Setting First Week for the Group?
articles.summary: This week's Five Burning Questions looks at a historic debut for the global pop group.
articles._body: It’s been a steady climb for the international girl group KATSEYE since its debut in 2024. This week, that ascent culminates with the group’s first-ever No. 1 on the Billboard 200 — with a historic first-week total. The five-track EP WILD bows atop the chart this week (dated Aug. 29) with 170,000 first-week units — not only marking the career-best performance for KATSEYE, whose 2025 EP Beautiful Chaos entered at No. 4 with 44,000 units, but also setting a new single-week high for an all-female group since the Billboard 200 switched to measuring albums in units in 2015. Meanwhile, the set’s new single “Hootie Frutti” debuts at No. 31 on the Billboard Hot 100, joining previous releases “Pinky Up” and “Animal” as the set’s third top 40 hit on the chart. How did KATSEYE manage such a massive debut? And are the group’s achievements being overshadowed by news about members going on hiatus? Billboard staffers and contributors discuss these questions and more below. 1. KATSEYE’s WILD debuts atop the Billboard 200 with 170,000 first-week units — the best-ever single-week number for an all-female group. On a scale from 1-10, how big a first-week performance is that for the group? Kyle Denis : A solid 7.5. Such a robust first week is certainly a testament to their pull despite the lineup drama and the wide range of opinions on their music.  Lyndsey Havens : 9 — and I’m only docking it a point because  WILD  is an EP, though I’ve since convinced myself that maybe it’s actually more impressive to have such a big first week with only five songs. So a 9.5, then. This debut feels especially triumphant given the year that KATSEYE has had; while there have been lows, like Manon announcing her hiatus in February and Sophia announcing hers this month, there have also been countless highs, from a huge Coachella debut to now earning the biggest single week for an all-women group. This feels like a nice feather in the girl group’s collective cap.  Andrew Unterberger : At least an 8. That first-week number — and particularly the 145,000 in pure sales it includes — suggests that the group has cultivated an extremely devoted fanbase, perhaps one further galvanized by the constant debate surrounding the group and its membership. Alicia Urrea : I’d definitely give it a 10/10. It’s hard to overstate how significant this is for KATSEYE; a No. 1 album would have been such an amazing achievement alone, but 170,000 units is genuinely such a historic opening. KATSEYE has gone from a No. 119 debut with  SIS (Soft Is Strong)  to No. 4 with  Beautiful Chaos  to No. 1 with  WILD  in just two years, so this feels like a major confirmation that the group’s fanbase has grown into an incredible force to be reckoned with.  Kristen Wisneski : I would rate it an 8. The girl group is truly a powerhouse, and its last EP, Beautiful Chaos (2025), debuted at No. 4 and featured multiple Hot 100 hits. Given that strong chart history, I’m not surprised that Wild debuted so successfully. But debuting at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 with 170,000 units sold is a phenomenal achievement and speaks to the dedication and strength of KATSEYE’s fanbase. Based on the trajectory so far, I’m confident the group will continue to grow and deliver even stronger music in the future. 2. The group’s 2025 set Beautiful Chaos bowed at No. 4 with 44,000 units moved — a little more than a quarter of the WILD debut number. What do you think the biggest reason is for the dramatically improved performance of this set? Kyle Denis : They simply raised their profile from virtually every possible angle. Since  Beautiful Chaos , the group picked up two Grammy nods and performed at the 2026 ceremony; played major sets at Coachella, Lollapalooza and Governor’s Ball, and won three American Music Awards. And, of course, Manon’s hiatus announcement, which sparked larger discourse about the treatment of Black members in mixed-race girl groups, helped the group land on the radars of those who would never give their music a second thought. When you combine all of this with each of the EP’s pre-release singles — “Pinky Up,” “Animal” and “Hootie Frutti” — spawning individual viral moments on socials, the improvement between  Beautiful Chaos  and  WILD  really isn’t that surprising.  Lyndsey Havens : Well, that’s the thing about having both highs and lows — they generate buzz all the same. I think interest in KATSEYE is reaching an all-time high, whether it be curiosity over the lineup changes and members’ wellbeing or a growing taste for the group’s brand of high-energy, sometimes sassy and always fierce brand of supercharged pop. Those are really nice ingredients that, when blended together, result in a recipe for the kind of moment they’re having right now.  Andrew Unterberger : As big as they were a year ago, in the past 12 months they’ve really become crossover stars — the kind that play the Grammys, score radio hits, go viral almost by default, and generally get themselves into the kind of spaces that most pop groups have been traditionally shut out of the past 10 years.
