articles.title: The Air Jordan 41 Came Straight Out of MJ’s Garage (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.summary: The Jordan team visited the Highsnobiety offices for an exclusive look at their newest shoe — and to spill on the basketball star’s involvement.
articles._body: A new mainline Air Jordan sneaker is to basketball as a new iPhone is to tech. This is not only the future of the most famous brand in town, but the future of hoop shoes as we know it. And yet, behind the gloss and sheen, there's a distinctly human element. And I'm not just talking about Michael Jordan (although His Airness was surprisingly involved with the new shoe's design). Although only two members of Jordan Brand visited the Highsnobiety offices in early August, brand-new Air Jordan 41 sneakers in tow — to their immense credit, they personally lugged the duffel bags full of sneakers and samples — they represent only a small fraction of the blood, sweat, and tears that informed the finished product. This is a shoe, yes, and a good fraction of Nike's quarterly report depends on it being a much-loved shoe. But it's also a testament to pure effort. So it goes for the entire line of flagship Jordan sneakers, and the man himself. Everything from the Air Jordan 1 up to this, the Air Jordan 41, represents much more than shoes. And so, when I spoke with Leo Chang, Senior Creative Director for Jordan Sport and Basketball, and Donald "DK" Kelsey, Senior Director of Jordan Basketball Footwear, I was initially more interested in talking about that under-sung human aspect. We all know the shoes. What about the hands behind the scenes? We still ended up discussing the sneaker at hand, but I'm glad we were able to dig a little deeper into one of sportswear's great achievements. Oh, and the Jordan 41's similarity to a Jordan 23 is pure happenstance: "You're not the first person to say that," laughs Chang. "But it's just one of those happy coincidences." Leo, let's start with you. Give me a little background that led to you working with Jordan Brand. Chang: I dreamt of working at Nike and Jordan when I was a kid. Growing up in Philadelphia, I was always an artist. I was probably drawing more than I talked and that combined with my love of sports naturally led me to really love sneakers. This was back in the '90s, which is one of the most revered eras of Nike and Jordan. I couldn't afford them but I had a lot of friends who had Air Jordans, the best Nikes. And now you've been there for 25 years. What're some of the projects you've overseen? Chang: People would know the work I've done across Nike basketball. KDs, early Kyries, I worked with Kobe a little bit, LeBron a little bit. Prior to that, I was on running, doing some of the Nike Frees, like the 3.0, 7.0, 5.0 V2s. I even did some Shox and had a hand in helping out the legendary Sergio Lozano on the Air Max 2003. Beautiful. So, DK, give us a little intro. DK: I'm originally from Chicago, so by default, I was a Chicago Bulls fan. And in terms of my biggest inspirations, I'll reference Allen Iverson, who gives credit to Michael Jordan. MJ was my north star. I've been with Nike for 19 years, the last 16 of which have been in product management. I've specifically been with Jordan Brand for almost 11 years and spent the first eight and a half in the retro business. And I'm one of the few product managers to have worked across all three product types in the company: footwear, apparel, and headwear. Any specific projects you want to call out people might recognize? DK: Well, it's a collaborative effort so it's tough to single anything out. But when I worked on hats, I was part of a great team that really expanded the line. If you think way back, no one really wore Nike hats. And I got to work on everything from signature basketball athlete hats, like Kobe and LeBron to NikeLab — if you remember that — where I oversaw collaborations with brands like Supreme and Nike ACG with Errolson [Hugh, founder of ACRONYM]. Perfect. So, you guys know product. Can you describe the feeling of knowing when something's "done?" Like, what makes a good product? Chang: I'm a big self-critic, and so I don't ever feel like the products are ever done. [laughs] But also, by the time we're at the end stages, I'm usually pretty tired of them. Something is done when it's performing well, it's testing well, the aesthetic is finishing nicely, and we're really sweating the details, like the colors and graphics. Once we're obsessing that, we're close to being ready to go. But you don't want to put out a mediocre product. You want to put out something you're proud of. That's been a really great learning, being like "Let's take a pause. It's not ready yet. Let's make sure it's right." What's something that might cause you to take a pause on a product? Chang: It could be pushing a new construction that's just not sitting right or maybe the upper's wrinkling weird. It could be an irritation point or heel slippage. It's a team effort. We gotta make sure that everyone. from marketing to design to engineering to development, is aligned enough to say that we might not hit a deadline. DK: There are so many people who add to a shoe. And it's my responsibility to make sure the expertise of the entire team is being poured into the project. Along with Leo, I protect the team and empower that. But we also have financial targets. The shoe has to make money. We'll collectively look at the cost options and be like, "OK, what's the hero item? What do we wanna save? What can we discard?" We have finance people in the room. They might be like, "We're $15 over target. What are we gonna do?" That's where creative comes in, that's where design comes in, and engineering comes in. Even when you're up against the clock, you've still gotta talk details. DK: We look at every single detail on the shoe. Every single one. On a shoe like this, it was like — well, take this rivet right her

articles.title: Your Fall Forecast Calls for a Serious Three-Stripes Intervention
articles.summary: adidas has everything you need to shake up your fall style, from wide-leg sweats and classic sneakers to statement track tops and graphic tees.
articles._body: Summer is officially on its way out, and while some will be mourning the loss of sandals and short-shorts, others (myself included) are more than ready for a gorgeously moody fall. With said new season comes the desire for an equally exciting wardrobe. We know it's gotta be comfortable , it’s gotta be snazzy, and most importantly, it’s gotta not chip too much into the savings account. Luckily, adidas ’ constant stream of new arrivals has everything you’ll need, and then some. We’re talking everything from layerable graphic tees, sweats and even a rogue pair of denim jeans. Like we said, this is your one-stop shop . Firebird Reversible Jacket A reversible jacket is always a good idea in theory. In practice, though, there’s usually one side you love and another you politely pretend doesn’t exist. adidas’ Firebird Reversible Coach Jacket is the rare exception. With two genuinely good looks to choose from, it’s essentially two jackets for the price of one. That alone makes getting dressed for fall a little easier. Superstar II The Superstar is a classic for a reason. Decades on, there’s still something about that shell toe and those three stripes that just works. This version doesn’t mess with a good thing either, keeping the formula familiar with just enough of a twist to make it feel fresh. Wide Leg Pants Come September, let’s face it, everyone’s going to need a wide-leg sweatpant. The temperature drops by about two degrees and suddenly the thought of wearing anything remotely restrictive feels deeply offensive. These adidas wide-leg pants are the perfect jumping-off point. Add the matching sweatshirt and voilà. Varsity Graphic Tee A tee might not be the first thing you’re reaching for this time of year, but that’s exactly why it deserves a spot in the rotation. Fall dressing is all about layers, after all, and you’re going to need something good underneath them. This varsity graphic tee does the job nicely. Consider it your autumn wardrobe’s supporting actor, quietly stealing the show. Full-Zip Sweatshirt And because no good pair of wide-leg sweatpants should have to go it alone, there’s the matching full-zip sweatshirt. Together, they make a strong case for spending September onwards in a coordinated sweatsuit. Denim Japan The Japan is one of those pairs you’ll probably wonder why you didn’t buy sooner. It has all the low-key appeal you want from an everyday sneaker , without feeling like you’ve reached for the same pair everyone else is wearing. Basically, if your Sambas need a little break come fall, this is where I’d look. Woven Barrel Pant Barrel leg pants aren’t going anywhere anytime soon, and thank goodness for that. There’s something about the shape that just works, giving you that slouchy, effortless silhouette without making you look like you’re swimming in fabric. These adidas ones are an easy win, particularly if you’re still getting used to the idea of a wider leg. Satin Polka Dot Track Top Polka dots are having a moment, and adidas has figured out how to make the trend actually wearable. This satin track top brings a little something extra to the classic track jacket without turning it into a one-fit wonder. The trick is pairing it with basics and letting the dots do the talking. Trendy? You bet. But wearable enough that you won’t be sick of looking at it by November. articles.title: Timberland’s Boat Mule Is Bigger than Yacht Season
articles.summary: Timberland's luxe suede boat shoe is a breezy slip-on that looks fit to walk on water.
articles._body: Timberland, known for hard-wearing work boots, has been making considerable strides in the leisure space. Having conquered loafers and clogs, Timberland is now flexing its mule muscle with the Classic Boat Mule, a simple suede slip-on that's designed for any number of maritime activities. The soft suede upper and moccasin-style stitching at the top reflect the sophisticated ease the work boot purveyor has grown quite fond of in recent years. Specifically, Timberland has been heavy in its preppy bag with courtyard-ready slip-ons like the Authentic Loafer or the canary yellow 3-Eye-Lug Boat Shoe , which represent a decidedly more collegiate side of Timberland's established style profile. Present-day, it's more than understood that Timberland does more than just its era-defining work boots, but this time the brand has taken things a step further by chopping the back half off a shoe altogether. Yes, Timberland flirts with excess from time to time, but in the case of the Classic Boat Mule, less really is more. Exposed heels in actual workwear settings? Absolutely not. On an easygoing slip-on mule, though? Well, there's just no other way to do it. Highsnobiety has affiliate marketing partnerships, which means we may receive a commission from your purchase. articles.title: Every Girl Wants to Dress Like Nhỏgirl
articles.summary: Every girl on TikTok is styling their Levi’s Engineered jeans the way Nhỏgirl’s Amy Pham Thi does — whether they know it or not.
articles._body: On a Saturday morning, a few hours before the first private shopping appointments begin, the vintage store Nhỏgirl has been turned into a photo studio. Tucked away along one of Amsterdam’s canals, the shop’s main room is stripped back to essentials: white walls, carefully arranged racks, and a table stacked with indie magazines. Overhead, a skylight lets in a wash of natural light that has come to define the Nhỏgirl aesthetic as much as the clothes themselves. Jade Ommen takes her place beneath it. She’s been one of the store’s recurring models since Nhỏgirl founder Amy Pham Thi approached her two years ago. Her hair is slicked into a bun, and she wears no visible makeup. She’s in a cashmere Prada top paired with timeworn trousers, their faded fabric and softened edges carrying the marks of previous wear. Ommen shifts her weight, slips her hands into her pockets, and lets her gaze drift to the camera. In this case, the camera is an iPhone. And the photographer is Pham Thi herself. Wearing no makeup, loose jeans, and an athletic sweatshirt so worn it looks like crêpe, she could just as easily be the one in front of the lens. Scroll through the Instagram pages of vintage stores in New York City, Copenhagen, Seoul, or Melbourne, and a pattern starts to emerge: a stripped-back interior, a white or beige wall, the bare, glowy face of a model. There’s often a poured concrete floor, and monochrome vintage and designer pieces hang from the girl just so. The light is natural, the camera setup simple, if there’s one at all. “Once you’ve seen that visual language enough times,” says Dakota Butler, a New York City–based creative consultant and Nhỏgirl customer, “you start recognizing it everywhere.” Many of these stores might not have consciously borrowed from Nhỏgirl. After all, the most pervasive aesthetics spread slowly, then suddenly seem to be everywhere at once. Nhỏgirl might not have been first — or it may have been. It certainly got there early. Levi’s Engineered jeans are now commonly referred to as “Nhỏgirl jeans,” while TikTok users routinely describe outfits — consisting of oversized sweaters, or vintage henleys and mini skirts — as “Nhỏgirl coded.” One vintage shop in an unassuming city is now a global reference point for cool-girl style. Within hours, one of Pham Thi’s images will appear on Nhỏgirl’s Instagram page. Although her business consists of a single appointment-only showroom in Amsterdam, the account has amassed more than 100,000 followers. Nhỏgirl’s posts are saved, reposted, and endlessly referenced — not only for the items on sale, but for the specific way the clothes are worn, combined, and framed. By the time many visitors step through the door of the store, they’ve been living in the Nhỏgirl world for months, sometimes years. They are no longer searching for one particular jacket or pair of trousers. They’re looking for a sensibility they already know by heart. “Calling it simply a vintage store doesn’t really give it enough credit,” Butler adds. “It’s a place where you can imagine another way of dressing.” ** Pham Thi did not come to fashion through retail. Born and raised in Berlin to Vietnamese parents, she trained as a dressmaker before moving into communication design, interested less in the garments themselves than in the ways images shape our understanding of them. “I was sewing, and I thought: I can’t even do a straight line,” she says, laughing. “There are people who are incredibly talented at that, and I realized I’m not one of them.” What attracted her instead was everything around the garment: the photography, the branding, the art direction. In short, the image-making. Which is why Nhỏgirl has never quite behaved like a store. When Pham Thi started Nhỏgirl in 2019, she wasn’t simply selling vintage but constructing a visual world. Her partner had already built a successful menswear business, rooted in the visual codes that dominated the time: loud graphics, streetwear, and logos. After moving to Amsterdam, Pham Thi joined him, initially helping with photography and styling. But she found herself gravitating toward softer silhouettes and a more minimal visual language. The solution was not to reinvent the existing business but to create a second one. Pham Thi launched Nhỏgirl as a parallel project, giving shape to the aesthetic she had been trying to introduce all along. In the beginning, the two ran both ventures side by side, surrounded by piles of clothing in a house that increasingly resembled a stockroom. “It was us, a simple white backdrop, and some cheap lights,” Pham Thi recalls. She describes those early creative decisions as instinctive rather than strategic. By now, she has refined the formula. Pham Thi avoids heavy makeup, obvious tattoos, or striking piercings on her models, removing anything that might compete with the garments themselves. Instead of minimalism, she speaks about tension. “I always like a bit of unease,” she says. “I’m drawn to things that clash.” A cashmere knit might be paired with a patched-up school jacket, or military surplus softened by sheer fabrics. Nothing is clipped or pinned to create the illusion of a perfect fit. A jacket may sit slightly oversized; a pair of trousers might hang lower than expected, revealing the waistband of a pair of underwear beneath. “I don’t mind that at all,” Pham Thi says. “I want the garment to fall the way it naturally falls on a body. If a thong is showing, that’s fine. I’m not trying to force clothes into an ideal shape.” The women she photographs are often braless beneath a sheer knit or lightweight top. Pham Thi sees a certain freedom in that kind of styling. “I like to show things as they are,” she says. From the outset, Nhỏgirl attracted an unexpectedly international audience. Pieces were auctioned through Instagram posts, with bidding wars unfolding in the comments and buyers setting alarms for the final hour. articles.title: Benito's Latest Signature Is Inspired By Crystal-Clear Coastal Waters
articles.summary: Dropping on September 26, 2026, the Bad Bunny x adidas Badbo 1.0 Night Navy delivers a moody iteration of the superstar's first ground-up signature model.
articles._body: Following a strong run of archival transformations on models like the Forum Low, Response CL, and Campus, Puerto Rican global icon Bad Bunny continues to expand his homegrown footwear universe. Dropping on September 26, 2026, the Bad Bunny x adidas Badbo 1.0 Night Navy delivers a moody iteration of the superstar's first ground-up signature model. What makes the Badbo 1.0 silhouette so significant is its status as a completely custom blueprint built specifically for Benito, rather than a standard retro recolor. Splicing Y2K basketball geometry, padded skate shoe proportions, and vintage indoor court tooling, the design mirrors Bad Bunny's eclectic personal aesthetic. The Night Navy colorway swaps out initial high-contrast palettes for a sophisticated, tonal gradient look inspired by the rich coastal waters surrounding his native Puerto Rico. Pairing multi-textured, dark blue suede with subtle performance details, the shoe strikes a balance between artistic storytelling and actually looking good. It’s a balance that a surprising number of releases can’t master. The upper is built from a mix of Night Navy suede, soft leather overlays, and perforated paneling. Strategic pops of bright orange at the top lace loops deliver sharp visual contrast against the deep blue backdrop, while Bad Bunny’s signature star emblem sits proudly on the heel. The shoe relies on a vintage-inspired off-white midsole that provides a slightly aged contrast to the upper's finish. Overall, the mixture of references across sports and eras means that this design is an amalgamation of Bad Bunny’s influences. Is that not exactly what a signature shoe should be? articles.title: Mark Gonzales (Once Again) Gives the Superstar Some Skate Cred
articles.summary: Mark Gonzales puts his skateboarding stamp on adidas’ iconic Superstar in a sleek triple-black colorway.
articles._body: The adidas Superstar has spent decades proving it can be just about anything to anyone. A basketball shoe turned hip-hop icon turned terrace staple, the shell-toed classic has never been particularly precious about where it hangs its hat. So, naturally, it makes perfect sense that Mark Gonzales got involved. The Superstar ADV x Gonz takes the familiar silhouette and gives it the skate treatment, without losing what made the original so good . This triple-black version keeps things relatively understated, with a leather upper and extra stitching built for life on and off a board. Of course, this is a Gonz collaboration, so there’s still a little mischief in the mix . His unmistakable creative touch gives the shoe some personality, even when the colorway is keeping things quiet. It’s a fitting partnership, really, and one that has been well received time after time. Gonz has spent his career making skateboarding look a little stranger and more interesting, while the Superstar has made a habit of adapting to whatever culture gets hold of it next. Together, they make a classic feel right at home somewhere new. A trick few icons can pull off. The SUPERSTAR ADV X GONZ is available on adidas' website for $100 now. articles.title: Why is Meta calling out TikTok and YouTube with a flurry of new ads? It's a game of 'reputational jujitsu.'
articles.summary: After a surprise multibillion-dollar settlement, Meta is going on the offensive against TikTok and YouTube in a new PR strategy.
articles._body: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg. Bloomberg/Getty Images Meta ran ads on social media and in print newspapers following a multibillion-dollar settlement. The advertisements call on TikTok and YouTube to join Meta in new protocols for teen safety. We spoke with PR pros about the upside and risks of this new PR strategy. Meta has a message for the public: Don't forget about TikTok and YouTube. After Meta's surprise settlement of up to $18 billion in a teen addiction lawsuit on Wednesday, the company is going on the offensive to shape the narrative with a series of ads on social media and in print newspapers. The advertisements, which Meta began running as a paid ad on its own platforms starting Wednesday, call for the two rival social media platforms to "join us in supporting teens." The ad links out to Meta's website announcing the settlement agreement. "We want to ensure teens benefit from this new industry standard, but we cannot do it alone," the blog post reads. "These protections will only be truly effective if we work with our peers — TikTok and YouTube — to put the same measures in place." Meta ran an ad on social media platforms and in print newspapers, calling on TikTok and YouTube. Screenshot/Instagram It's true that Meta's Instagram and Facebook apps aren't the only social media apps under scrutiny for how teens use them. It's also true that Meta's messaging is a useful public relations strategy in the wake of a year fraught with legal battles . Mark Borkowski, a UK-based public-relations consultant, called Meta's advertisements an attempt at "reputational jujitsu." We asked PR pros, including Borkowski, what they made of Meta's latest move. A potential win-win for Meta "This is actually quite a clever move from Meta," Sam Gauchier, a brand and communications consultant, told Business Insider. "They've put TikTok and YouTube in a position where almost any response benefits them." If TikTok and YouTube follow suit, Meta can take credit for the public pressure it exerted on the two platforms, Gauchier said. If the platforms don't, Meta could benefit from appearing to be the good guy. "On paper, Meta's taking a 'shared responsibility' approach," comms consultant Michael Draznin said. "It's designed so Meta keeps a perceived industry leadership role either way." Motivation is in the eye of the beholder A key part of Meta's settlement agreement is implementing limits for how teens use apps like Instagram. Teens will be limited to 2 hours a day on Meta's apps, have access blocked at night, and get adjusted notifications. The apps will also add more parental controls. If teens are barred from using Instagram for hours on end, where will they go instead? Borkowski said that Meta has a "clear commercial interest in ensuring competitors inherit the same costs and constraints." Ad dollars could flow to TikTok and YouTube instead, Forrester principal analyst Kate Winick said. Meta said that teens account for less than 1% of its overall revenue and that, on average, US teens spend about 1 hour a day on Instagram. Meta will also pay an additional $5.3 billion — on top of the baseline $12.7 billion — if TikTok and YouTube agree to implement product changes for teens and make their own settlements of $5.3 billion each. Still, perception is the name of the game in PR. "Had they first taken accountability, shown real humility and started to make progress on their agreements, I think a stronger public push for the rest of the industry — not just singling out TikTok and YouTube — could have helped them rebuild a bit of trust with parents and the public," PR consultant Sarah Gooding said. "Instead, their letter came off as self-serving and insincere." It's going to be a marathon, not a sprint This isn't the first time Meta's reputation has been in hot water. It often takes time, and ultimately, substantial changes to shift public opinion about a brand. Borkowski said that "the proof will be in the pudding" in how much Facebook and Instagram actually change. Meta's strategy isn't a surefire path to redemption. "Could it backfire? Of course," Forrester's Winick said. "We're talking here about a company that has an immense amount of public sentiment already against it." That said, calling for industry changes — especially by putting rivals in the spotlight — could force social media companies to get on the same page. Winick said that Meta's biggest PR win will come "if they can make consumers stop and think and say, 'You know what? It's not just Instagram that's the problem.'" articles.title: These states have produced the most Miss USA winners
articles.summary: The 75th annual Miss USA pageant will take place in Miami on August 27, so we looked back at the states that have had the most success.
articles._body: Some states have dominated the Miss USA pageant over its 74-year history. Ethan Miller/Getty Images The 75th annual Miss USA pageant will take place in Miami on August 27. Some states have had far more success than others at the competition. Texas has the most Miss USA wins, taking the crown 10 times. The United States has the most winners in Miss Universe history , but which states reign supreme when it comes to Miss USA ? One state had a five-year winning streak and produced two future Miss Universe winners . Meanwhile, 18 states still haven't won the crown. They'll get a chance to change their record at the 75th annual Miss USA pageant in Miami on August 27. Until then, let's take a look back at the most successful states in the history of the Miss USA pageant . Texas has won the Miss USA crown 10 times. Josh Brasted/Getty Images Texas has a storied history in the world of pageants. Two Miss Texas winners who won Miss USA went on to win Miss Universe: Chelsi Smith and R'Bonney Gabriel . Miss Texas 2008 Crystle Stewart , who also won Miss USA, served as CEO and president of the Miss USA and Miss Teen USA pageants from 2020 to 2023. Texas won five Miss USA pageants in a row from 1985 to 1989, a streak nicknamed the "Texas Aces." The full list of Miss Texas titleholders who won Miss USA is: 1977: Kimberly Tomes 1985: Laura Martinez Herring 1986: Christy Fichtner 1987: Michelle Royer 1988: Courtney Gibbs 1989: Gretchen Polhemus 1995: Chelsi Smith 2001: Kandace Krueger 2008: Crystle Stewart 2022: R'Bonney Gabriel California, which has taken the Miss USA crown six times, is catching up. VALERIE MACON/AFP via Getty Images California has won a Miss USA title in every decade except the 2000s. Its most recent winner was Alyssa Campanella, who took the crown in 2011. The full list of Miss California titleholders who won Miss USA is: 1959: Terry Huntingdon 1966: Maria Remenyi 1975: Summer Bartholomew 1983: Julie Hayek 1992: Shannon Marketic 2011: Alyssa Campanella Hawaii assumed its fifth Miss USA title after Miss USA 2023 Noelia Voigt resigned, a first in the pageant's history. Gilbert Flores/Variety via Getty Images Miss Hawaii 1962 Macel Wilson became the first woman from Hawaii to enter the Miss USA competition, as well as the first Asian American and first woman of color to win the crown. Miss Hawaii 1997 Brook Lee won both Miss USA and Miss Universe. The state assumed its fifth title after Miss USA 2023 Noelia Voigt stepped down three months before her reign came to an end due to the leadership of Laylah Rose , who was CEO of Miss USA at the time. Miss Hawaii Savannah Gankiewicz , who had won first runner-up at the pageant, took Voigt's place. The full list of Miss Hawaii titleholders who were named Miss USA is: 1962: Macel Wilson 1972: Tanya Wilson 1978: Judi Andersen 1997: Brook Lee 2023: Savannah Gankiewicz Multiple states have four winners, including Michigan. Alberto E. Rodriguez/Getty Images Carole Gist was both the first Miss Michigan and the first African American woman to win the Miss USA crown. In 2010, Miss Michigan Rima Fakih made history as the first Arab American woman to take the title. Former Miss Michigan Kenya Moore, who won Miss USA in 1993, has become one of the most famous contestants in the pageant's history after starring in "The Real Housewives of Atlanta" from 2012 to 2025. The most recent Miss Michigan to win Miss USA is Alma Cooper , a US Army officer who took the crown in 2024. The full list of Miss Michigan titleholders who won Miss USA is: 1990: Carole Gist 1993: Kenya Moore 2010: Rima Fakih 2024: Alma Cooper The District of Columbia's recent Miss USA titles came in quick succession. Ethan Miller/Getty Images The District of Columbia doesn't have representation in the Senate, but it sure does well on the Miss USA stage. In 2016, Deshauna Barber won Miss District of Columbia, and Kára McCullough placed first runner-up. Barber went on to win Miss USA, while McCullough won Miss District of Columbia in 2017. That year, Barber crowned McCullough the new Miss USA. It was the first time a place had won back-to-back Miss USA titles since the Texas Aces' reign. The full list of Miss District of Columbia titleholders who won Miss USA is: 1964: Bobbi Johnson 2002: Shauntay Hinton 2016: Deshauna Barber 2017: Kára McCullough Illinois has also taken the Miss USA title four times, but all its wins came before 1975. Bettmann/Getty Images Illinois is also one of only four states to win back-to-back Miss USA titles. The full list of Miss Illinois titleholders who won Miss USA is: 1953: Myrna Hansen 1963: Marite Ozers 1973: Amanda Jones 1974: Karen Morrison New York has the honor of winning the very first Miss USA pageant. CBS via Getty Images Miss New York 1952 Jackie Loughery was named the very first Miss USA. She also represented the USA at the first-ever Miss Universe pageant that same year, placing in the top 10. New York assumed its third Miss USA crown in 1995, when Shanna Moakler inherited the title after Chelsi Smith won Miss Universe 1995. The full list of Miss New York titleholders who won Miss USA is: 1952: Jackie Loughery 1979: Mary Therese Friel 1995: Shanna Moakler 1999: Kimberly Ann Pressler All four of North Carolina's wins have been during the 2000s. Paras Griffin/Getty Images North Carolina has really hit its stride on the pageant stage in recent years. The state's most recent Miss USA title came when Morgan Romano assumed the 2022 crown after R'Bonney Gabriel won America's ninth Miss Universe title. The full list of Miss North Carolina titleholders who won Miss USA is: 2005: Chelsea Cooley 2009: Kristen Dalton 2019: Cheslie Kryst 2022: Morgan Romano Read the original article on Business Insider

articles.title: OpenAI issues call for 'collective action' on cyber defense: 'We have a limited window'
articles.summary: More than 100 organizations, including Anthropic, joined OpenAI's call for action.
articles._body: OpenAI called on governments to strengthen cyber defenses before it is too late. SeongJoon Cho/Bloomberg via Getty Images OpenAI issued a stark cybersecurity warning on Thursday. The AI giant wrote in an open letter that "AI-enabled cyber attacks" will become more widespread. More than 100 organizations, including Anthropic, joined OpenAI's call for collective action. OpenAI says there's a "limited window to strengthen cyber defenses." More than 100 organizations joined OpenAI in an open letter calling for companies and governments to strengthen cybersecurity defenses before it's too late. Of particular note, rival Anthropic is one of the signatories, a sign that even the two biggest AI companies can find common ground. "In the coming months, AI-enabled cyber attacks will become far more widespread and sophisticated as models around the world become increasingly capable," the company wrote in an open letter. "The companies and public services our communities depend on—from hospitals to water treatment plants to the infrastructure that powers the internet—are at risk." OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said, "There is not much time to act." "this is a critically important moment for cyber defense with AI; there is not much time to act," Altman wrote on X. "we are happy if you want to work with us or any of our competitors or partners, but please take this moment seriously. only an urgent and intense collective response will work." The letter comes as OpenAI continues to disclose information about how rogue agents broke out of what was presumed to be a secure testing environment before hacking into Hugging Face in search of answers to cheat on internal testing. Altman had portrayed the breach as a watershed moment. "This is the first security incident that I have felt very viscerally," Altman said during a recent interview. The letter lays out suggestions for organizations, cybersecurity companies, governments, and frontier AI companies. The recommendations include calling on governments to better fund cyber defense, asking cybersecurity companies to share "threat intelligence and tested playbooks," and urging AI labs to "share tools, playbooks, and credible threat assessments" with those who need it the most. "We call on leaders across industry and government to bring the full weight of their technology, resources, and expertise to this effort," the letter reads. "Put cyber-capable AI in the hands of defenders, starting with the teams protecting essential services." Other notable tech signatories include Microsoft, Google, Amazon Web Services, Oracle, Cisco, IBM, and CrowdStrike. Hugging Face, the victim of OpenAI's breach, also signed. A number of notable companies are also part of the group, including Citi, General Motors, Visa, Capitol One, Mastercard, and Citadel. You can read the full open letter here . articles.title: Nvidia's interest in Hugging Face is a hedge against a future dominated by OpenAI and Anthropic
articles.summary: Nvidia had talks to acquire Hugging Face for $13 billion, Business Insider reported. It could boost Nvidia's open-source strategy, challenging OpenAI.
articles._body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Jung Yeon-je / AFP via Getty Images Nvidia's interest in Hugging Face supercharges its push into open-source AI. Open models could keep OpenAI and Anthropic from gaining too much power and squeezing Nvidia out. While Nvidia could gain more control over Hugging Face, too much could backfire. What does $13 billion buy Nvidia these days? A bigger say in what AI gets built and what it runs on. Business Insider reported on Wednesday that the chip giant was in talks to acquire Hugging Face , which hosts open-source AI models. That lines up with Nvidia's strategy as of late, as it has been beating the drum about open-source AI — models that anyone can use and build on. Open models could stave off a future dominated by giants like OpenAI and Anthropic, both of which create closed, proprietary models. If top AI labs dominate the models being used and build their own chips to run them — as OpenAI is doing with Jalapeño — they could eventually cut Nvidia out. "Open source is an important counterweight to closed platforms like OpenAI and Anthropic," said Brad Gastwirth, global head of research and market intelligence at Circular Technology. "The more AI development stays open and fragmented across many models and developers, the more opportunity Nvidia has to remain the underlying infrastructure provider." There's a more immediate payoff, too: selling more chips. Developers using models from Hugging Face have to decide which hardware and software to run them on, and owning the hub could give Nvidia more sway over their choices. Neither Nvidia nor Hugging Face immediately responded to requests for comment from Business Insider. Nvidia could get more control over open-source AI Nvidia has been circling Hugging Face for years. It joined a $235 million funding round in 2023, and it distributes its own family of open models, Nemotron, on Hugging Face. Last year, Nvidia proposed a $500 million investment in Hugging Face at a $7 billion valuation, which the startup rejected, the Financial Times reported. Hugging Face said at the time it didn't want a single investor wielding too much influence. That's because one of its hallmarks is its openness, with models that run on competing chips and cloud companies, including AMD and Google. That makes a possible Nvidia acquisition a striking reversal, and it creates a tricky balance. "The biggest risk is neutrality," Gastwirth said. "Hugging Face has a lot of value because developers see it as an open platform. Nvidia would have to be careful not to undermine that." While Nvidia could get greater control over Hugging Face, it may have to use that control sparingly to preserve the openness that makes the startup so valuable. Have a tip? articles.title: Trump signs executive order to rename Lake Ontario 'Lake America'
articles.summary: President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Thursday, which he says officially renames the lake.
articles._body: He said the change only requires "a good pen and some intelligence." Jim WATSON / AFP via Getty Images Trump on Thursday signed an executive order, which he said "immediately" changed the name of a Great Lake. It's now "Lake America," not "Lake Ontario," Trump said. The move is the latest escalation between the feuding neighbors. President Donald Trump 's fight with Canada has spilled into Lake Ontario — er, Lake America? On Thursday, Trump signed an executive order that he said would "immediately" rename the body of water to "Lake America." Canadian officials have said they will not recognize the new name. The order directs the US government to adopt "Lake America" as the official name used on federal maps and in federal contracts and documents. It does not require private map providers to adopt the change. Apple and Google didn't immediately respond to questions about whether they would update their maps. The move comes as relations between Washington and Ottawa rapidly deteriorate . Trade talks between the neighboring countries broke down on Friday, which prompted new tariffs from the US. Canada responded with its own tariffs, while Trump is threatening potential 50% tariffs on auto and steel imports from Canada, set for January 1. Trump had threatened to rename the lake several times since the tensions flared. In a video posted to Truth Social, Trump said renaming the lake only required "a good pen and some intelligence," while crossing out the name on a paper map. "We're on it, Mr. President," Interior Secretary Doug Burgum wrote on X . "The places and waters that border our nation and support our economy should reflect the greatness of the United States." He's already published a secretarial order to the Board on Geographic Names to "immediately rename the body of water known as Lake Ontario to Lake America." Several Democratic leaders mocked the renaming. Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers posted a video of himself signing a restaurant napkin that declared Lake Michigan "Lake Wisconsin." "See, I can sign napkins that say things, too," he wrote . New York Gov. Kathy Hochul had a blunter response. New York won’t be calling it that. https://t.co/FJQonEk8tI — Governor Kathy Hochul (@GovKathyHochul) August 27, 2026 The lake — whichever name you give it — runs along New York State's northwest and Ontario's southwest borders. It's the smallest of the Great Lakes by surface area. In the executive order, the US said it invested nearly $4 billion in "protecting the Great Lakes freshwater ecosystem in the last decade," including providing nine of the eleven ice-breaking vessels. It's the second time that Trump has renamed a major body of water during his second term. In January 2025, he signed an executive order to rename the "Gulf of Mexico" the " Gulf of America. articles.title: My mom has Alzheimer's, and my kids are young. Forget the 'sandwich generation' — I feel like I'm in a panini press.
articles.summary: I'm a mom and an Alzheimer's caregiver. Being everyone's emergency contact means juggling appointments, finances, medications, and constant uncertainty.
articles._body: Catherine and her mom together at Catherine's wedding. Courtesy of the author I manage responsibilities for my children while helping care for my aging mother. Alzheimer's adds anticipatory grief to an already overwhelming mental load. I've found support from other women facing the same multigenerational caregiving squeeze. My daughter had just turned 7 years old. Her one request was that we host a birthday party at our house. My husband and I agreed and started preparing. Like many parents, we needed a little help managing the moving pieces. I asked my mother if she wouldn't mind watching my oldest daughter and our dog during the party. My mom was diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease in 2025. She still lives independently, with support, but loves seeing her granddaughters. She agreed, and we decided I would drop off my daughter and my dog with her before the party. When I opened the door to my mom's apartment, I immediately realized something was wrong. She was lying on the floor , unable to get up. I quickly called 911 and let my husband know that I would not be returning for my daughter's party. Thankfully, after more than 12 hours in the emergency room, my mom was able to return home. But I was crushed by guilt . I had missed my younger daughter's party, and the experience of seeing my mom so debilitated was deeply upsetting for my older daughter to witness. The 'sandwich generation' doesn't capture the pressure I feel People often call this the " sandwich generation ": adults caught between raising children and caring for their aging parents. But increasingly, I have heard another phrase that feels more accurate: the "panini generation." Catherine, her brother, and her mom in front of the restaurant that their family used to run. Courtesy of the author A sandwich is stacked neatly. But my life often feels like it is being pressed from every side, under heat, with very little room to move. For those of us raising children while caring for parents, moments like this are not rare interruptions. They are part of the reality we are constantly trying to manage. Alzheimer's makes caregiving feel impossible to compartmentalize Firsthand experience has taught me that Alzheimer's intensifies that pressure in ways that are hard to fully grasp until you live it. It is a progressive disease that requires increasing supervision. It brings emotional strain, not just from the physical demands of care, but from memory loss and personality changes that reshape relationships over time. Losing my mother bit by bit is heart-wrenching. And it unfolds over years, adding a layer of anticipatory grief and emotional strain on top of one of the most demanding periods of my life as a mother and a professional. Catherine and her mom laughing at Catherine's wedding dinner. Courtes of the author While this reality affects families broadly, women often bear the brunt. We carry the majority of Alzheimer's caregiving responsibilities, while also facing a higher lifetime risk of developing the disease ourselves. That dual reality makes this not just a caregiving issue, but a personal health issue. The women who join me in this "panini generation" are simultaneously managing careers and financial responsibilities, raising children, caring for aging parents, and navigating midlife health changes that can impact their own brain health. We are the stabilizing force across generations, often at a cost that isn't visible in the moment. Caregivers often face reduced income or career disruption, rising out-of-pocket care costs, and competing priorities between children, parents, and their own long-term security. One particularly difficult piece for me is the intense mental load that comes with being the command center for everyone: organizing doctors' visits, medications, finances, transportation, and social engagements. I am everyone's emergency contact, if and when something goes wrong. My mom is still herself Nearly two years into my mom's Alzheimer's diagnosis, she's still herself — sharp in so many ways, funny, and stubborn. But caregiving has become a bigger part of my life, and I know that will only continue to grow. What has helped me navigate that uncertainty is finding community with other women who are carrying many of the same responsibilities — caring for aging parents while raising children, managing careers, and trying to remain present for the people they love. There is comfort in being understood without having to explain, but there is also urgency in realizing just how many of the women I've met along the way are stretched thin by systems that were never designed for this reality. Workplaces have not kept pace with long-term, multigenerational caregiving. Community resources remain limited. And proactive brain health education, especially during midlife, is still inadequate. The women I have met throughout this journey remind me that no caregiver should have to reach a breaking point before finding support. Catherine Patterson is the acting Chief Operating Officer of UsAgainstAlzheimer's. Read the original article on Business Insider

articles.title: Dollar General is adding more $1 items. It's stealing a page from supermarkets' playbook
articles.summary: Dollar General boosts $1 items by 40% ahead of the holidays, after second-quarter success. Strategy targets increasing foot traffic.
articles._body: Dollar General plans to increase its selection of $1 items by the end of the year. Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images Dollar General is adding more $1 items to its stores, executives said Thursday. The dollar store chain plans to increase its $1 selection by 40% in time for the holidays. Dollar General is doubling down on the price point after second-quarter sales success Dollar General is doubling down on the $1 price point . A selection of 600 items priced at $1 each, which the chain calls "Value Valley," had comparable sales growth of 16% during the company's second quarter — a much faster clip than broader same-store sales growth of 3.5%, it said on Thursday. In total, Dollar General stocks about 2,000 items that cost $1 each. It expects to grow that number by 40% in the second half of 2026 in time for the holiday shopping season, COO Emily Taylor said on the retailer's earnings call. Expect that selection to grow "even more so into 2027," CEO Todd Vasos said. "We have got real plans to expand that $1 price point to offer even more value for the consumer," he added. Dollar stores used to be true to their name, with everything on their shelves priced at $1. Inflation has changed that, though: In 2021, Dollar Tree raised prices on most items to $1.25 and has since experimented with items priced at several dollars each. That's a different direction than Dollar General appears to be taking, said Arielle Feger, a senior analyst at EMARKETER, Business Insider's sister company. While Dollar General has long sold items that cost well over $1 each, many of those items are food and other consumables that draw people into the store, Feger said. The chain began adding freezers stocked with food items priced at $1 each to its stores earlier this year, Vasos said on the company's last earnings call in June. Dollar Tree's $1 item selection, by contrast, skews more toward discretionary items, such as home decor and toys. Dollar General's strategy is similar to the classic grocery store strategy of selling eggs and milk as cheaply as possible — even at a loss, potentially — to boost overall sales, Feger said. "It gets people in the door, and it gets them to continue to come back," she said. That strategy is particularly meaningful to customers who are trying to save money, Vasos said on Thursday's earnings call. Dollar General's average customer is "still gainfully employed" and "is seeing some gains in her income levels," the CEO said. But inflation and rising gas prices this year have offset that income gain, Vasos said, leading many customers to visit its stores more often and buy less each trip. By expanding its selection of $1 items, Dollar General will likely continue to attract customers, Feger said. "Consumers are habitual," she said. "We go to the same places, we expect the same things." Do you have a story idea about Dollar General or Dollar Tree? articles.title: A social media app that feels like the old Instagram days raised $21 million
articles.summary: In 2023, ex-Instagram employees launched a new app called Retro. It's one of many new social media apps taking on Big Tech platforms.
articles._body: Retro is a social media app for sharing content with friends and family. Screenshot/Retro/BI Retro, designed by ex-Instagram employees, is a social app for sharing content with close friends. The startup behind it has raised $21 million, recent financial filings reveal. It's one of many new social media apps taking on Big Tech platforms. There's a social media app I like using more than Instagram or TikTok — and it's attracted serious investor interest. The app, called Retro, is an Instagram alternative for sharing photos and videos with close friends or family. The startup behind the app, Lone Palm Labs, has raised at least $21 million in venture capital funding, according to recent financial filings viewed by Business Insider. On the startup's website, the company lists investors such as Josh Kushner's Thrive Capital , Scribble Ventures, Imaginary Ventures, and Uncommon Projects , as well as angels including Figma CEO Dylan Field. Retro did not respond to requests for comment. Retro was founded by former Instagram employees who wanted to build a "super simple product that's really just for you and your friends," Nathan Sharp, Lone Palm's CEO, previously told Business Insider. Sharp, who worked on both Instagram and Facebook, teamed up with Ryan Olson, a longtime Instagram engineer, in 2022 to found Lone Palm Labs. Split between New York and San Francisco, Lone Palm Labs is a team of seven employees, according to the company's website. The company launched another app in 2025, called Splat, which can make a coloring page for kids from photos using AI. While venture capital is pouring money into AI, data centers, and SaaS companies, some consumer tech startups building social media apps have had to fight tooth and nail to get a slice of the pie. PitchBook data revealed a steady decline in the number of deals backing social startups since a peak in 2021 — though total deal value for 2026 is already rebounding after a dismal 2025. That environment makes Lone Palm Labs' haul especially notable. Social media for your real-life friends Since Retro launched in 2023, the social app has added many new features. While it's primarily a diary for documenting your daily life — I typically share photos and memes from the week — it's expanded with shared photo albums and a feed of throwbacks that transport you back in time via your camera roll. You can also send posts from the app as literal postcards in the mail. Unlike Instagram or Facebook, I don't have hundreds of friends added on the app. I have a lean social graph of 20 friends. According to data from market intelligence firm Sensor Tower, Retro has an estimated 1.7 million global monthly active users and 7.8 million global downloads as of Wednesday. Outside the US, the app has seen success in countries such as Japan, Taiwan, Germany, and Spain, according to Appfigures data. Retro users pay about $36 a year for premium. Screenshots/Retro The app currently has no ads and uses a freemium model for monetization. While it's free to make an account, Retro in 2025 introduced a premium subscription that lets users unlock features such as posting videos and viewing other friends' content without having to post their own. The subscription costs about $36 a year. As bigger social media apps lose their social-ness and become more entertainment platforms, apps like Retro are betting that people are willing to pay for connection. articles.title: Meta memo reveals what its new 'Hatch' AI agent can do, from booking a restaurant to finding a dog sitter
articles.summary: Meta told staff its Hatch AI agent "can do anything you can do online" and will be highly personal to the user.
articles._body: CEO Mark Zuckerberg says Meta is building "personal superintelligence for everyone." Bloomberg/Getty Images Meta said its coming Hatch AI agent "can do anything you can do online." Meta has been testing Hatch with employees, per an internal memo. Hatch can "remember more than most AIs," the memo said. It can DJ. It can order food. It can book you a table at a restaurant. And of course, it can access your Instagram. These are some things Meta says its coming AI agent can do, according to an internal memo seen by Business Insider. Known internally as "Project Hatch," the new agent is Meta's answer to OpenClaw , the autonomous AI assistant that went viral earlier this year as companies increasingly bet on AI capable of performing tasks rather than just answering queries. A product manager told staff in an internal channel last month that Hatch was being made available to employees outside its Meta Superintelligence Labs group for testing. The memo described Hatch as "a personal agent that's always working on your behalf to help achieve your goals and improve your life, your health, your relationships, your personal finances and more." The memo to staff included a list of things Hatch could do. "It has its own computer so it can do anything you can do online, like filling out forms, buying something, or performing deep research," it said, in a section titled "What makes Project Hatch different from an AI assistant?" Meta is positioning Hatch as a general consumer product capable of performing a range of computer-based tasks, at a time when generalist agents are taking off. Google launched a similar tool, Gemini Spark , earlier this year, while OpenAI and Anthropic also have agents capable of controlling users' computers . A new AI assistant from the startup Instinct, which users can call or text, has also generated buzz in recent weeks. Hatch could become a new way for Meta to make money from its AI investments. While the company has been working to catch rivals with new models and a new coding agent , its AI revenue has mostly come from improvements to its advertising products. It could not be learned what Meta plans to charge for Hatch or an exact launch timeline. The Information previously reported that Meta plans to launch Hatch in the next few weeks and that it has considered charging up to $200 a month for it. A Meta spokesperson declined to comment. Meta wants to crack the AI agent market The memo said Hatch can connect directly to apps such as email and calendar, and gave Spotify, Instagram, and OpenTable as examples. "It has great memory and can remember more than most AIs," the memo read, adding that users can "approve any sensitive actions" before they happen. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has previously touted his vision of a future in which everyone has their own personal AI assistants capable of performing tasks. "Meta is the company primarily focused on building personal superintelligence for everyone," he said in a manifesto earlier this month. The memo said that Hatch would be highly personal to the user. "You design your agent, so no two are alike. You name it, shape how it talks and decide what it pays attention to. If it gets something wrong, tell it and it adjusts," the memo said. The product manager who posted the note said they had built a Hatch agent named Veda that had helped them find a new dog sitter, purchase a Father's Day gift, and change their sleep habits. Hatch also works in the background "even when the app is closed," the memo added. Have something to share? Contact this reporter via email at hlangley@businessinsider.com or Signal at 628-228-1836. articles.title: Ukraine says Russia used its upgraded, longer-range 'Iskander-1000' missile in a bombardment of Kyiv
articles.summary: Russia fired the upgraded, longer-range ballistic missile during a recent combined strike on Kyiv, Ukraine said.
articles._body: Russia's been upgrading its ballistic missile arsenal, making the weapons more difficult for Ukrainian air defenses to intercept. Contributors/Getty Images Russia fired a new ballistic missile during a recent strike on Ukraine. The Iskander-1000 has a larger engine and longer range than its predecessor. Russia has been upgrading its ballistic missile arsenal, threatening Ukraine's already strained air defenses. Russia fired an upgraded version of its Iskander short-range ballistic missile for the first time in a summer strike on the Ukrainian capital city, the country's military intelligence agency shared this week. Russian forces have significantly ramped up their ballistic missile attacks on Ukraine this year. These strikes come as Russia upgrades its arsenal and Ukraine struggles to procure sufficient numbers of critical air-defense interceptors. On Thursday, Ukraine's GUR, the country's military and defense intelligence agency, said that Russia had used an upgraded ballistic missile , the 9M723-2 or "Iskander-1000," against Ukraine for the first time during a complex bombardment of Kyiv this summer. The Iskander-1000 is an upgraded variant of the 9M723-1, a ballistic missile fired by Russia's Iskander system, with a larger engine and launcher that extend its range. Ukraine has assessed that these modifications have increased its maximum range to about 340 miles, about 100 miles farther than its predecessor. It added that most other components remain the same. The first combat use of the Iskander-1000 highlights Russia's ongoing investments in expanding and improving its ballistic missile arsenal. Ukrainian officials have said such weapons are becoming an increasingly prominent part of Moscow's strike campaign . The additional range on the upgraded 9M723-2 missile allows Russian Iskander launchers to operate from farther back while still threatening Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities. US-made Patriot systems are Ukraine's top choice for intercepting Russian ballistic missiles. US Army photo Ukraine has tracked evolutions in Russian ballistic missile technology , including changes in maneuverability that make the weapons more difficult to intercept. These developments have at times challenged Ukrainian air defenses, such as the US-made MIM-104 Patriot surface-to-air missile system . Last fall, for instance, a US defense intelligence assessment found that Ukraine's Patriots struggled to consistently intercept Russian ballistic missiles due to certain recent "tactical improvements" Moscow had made to the weapons. The Patriot is a top-tier air defense platform in Ukraine and is considered its best defense against Russian ballistic missiles like the Iskander and the air-launched Kh-47M2 Kinzhal, but it's not infallible. Right now, though, Ukraine is running low on interceptor missiles. Some nights, Ukraine hasn't been able to intercept a single missile . Russia has also expanded its arsenal with assistance from North Korea. Earlier this month, the Ukrainian Air Force said North Korea's KN-23 missile , which is a rough copy of Russia's Iskander missile, had been used in two strikes. Ukrainian and Western officials have assessed that ongoing military cooperation between North Korea and Russia has allowed both countries to improve their weapons and technologies. articles.title: Jensen Huang says AI data centers can fix the very grid they’re straining
articles.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said the US can't afford to miss out on AI advancements.
articles._body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says the entire AI ecosystem has "to do a much better job working with the communities" on data centers. Bloomberg/Getty Images Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says the industry has to do a "better" job working with communities. Huang is the latest voice in tech to acknowledge that something has to change. Polling shows many in the US have turned hard against data center construction. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says the AI industry needs to do "better" when it comes to data centers. "The technology industry, the builders, and, have to do a much better job working with the communities to get prepared for this AI infrastructure build-out," Huang told CNBC's Jim Cramer on Wednesday when asked about how Nvidia's customers could show communities they are serious about data center concerns. Huang is the latest voice in tech, and arguably the biggest so far, to acknowledge that the industry has to do a better job of selling communities on building data centers. Polling shows that Americans have become deeply skeptical of the massive facilities that house the advanced chips that train and serve AI demand. Huang said the industry needs to sell the idea that data center construction can help reindustrialize the nation. Addressing a frequent concern, Huang said data centers could actually lower energy costs. "It is also the case this is the first time in probably the last century that we're able to invest in sustainable energy, invest in improving our energy grid, securing our energy supply, reducing the cost of energy across the country," he said. "This is the first time in history that we're able to do that because of the enormous market dynamics, the market forces that are able to invest in the energy ecosystem." Business Insider has previously reported that rapid data center expansion could increase electricity costs . A recent study by researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology found that data centers could reduce consumer costs by adjusting their power consumption. The MIT researchers found that data centers that shift their power consumption to off-peak hours could lower average energy costs by up to 4% in the Mid-Atlantic, 5% in Texas, and 2% in 11 western states compared to facilities that didn't change their consumption patterns. The researchers studied power grids in each of those three areas due to the prevalence of data centers there. There is a big caveat to their findings. The researchers said that under some scenarios, data centers would need to shift nearly 50% of their energy consumption to non-peak hours, such as the afternoon. On Wednesday, Nvidia reported that data center revenue totaled $89 billion in the second quarter of FY 26, up 117% from a year ago. The figure also surpassed Wall Street's estimates, illustrating just how lucrative the broader AI buildout is for the world's largest company by market cap. Like President Donald Trump , Huang warned of the costs to the US if data centers aren't built out. "We have to make sure that our communities, our society, all of our companies, all of our people in the United States embrace this technology so that we can take advantage of what this technology could do for all of our ecosystems, all of our economy, and all of our societies," Huang said. He added, "Otherwise, we're going to get left behind." At the same time, the vibes in the US look increasingly dour. Governors have moved to pump the brakes on data center construction amid a growing public backlash. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott , who is seeking reelection, imposed an effective moratorium on new data center construction until state agencies complete a comprehensive audit. Abbott was rather blunt about how he went from declaring Texas the "epicenter of AI development" to imposing a moratorium in less than a year. "They basically dug their own grave for the problem that's been caused for them, and that's why they got the backlash they deserve," Abbott said during an interview on ABC's "This Week." articles.title: We could all learn something from Olympic champion Alysa Liu’s commitment to rest
articles.summary: It's not uncommon for a public figure to take a break from work for health reasons. Olympic champion Alysa Liu is taking one before things get bad.
articles._body: Alysa Liu is not competing in the 2026 to 2027 figure skating season. Tang Xinyu/VCG via Getty Images Alysa Liu is taking another step back from competitive figure skating. In 2022, she quit because she was miserable. This time, she's breaking to 'fine-tune' her skating. It could be a step towards normalizing resting before you're so exhausted your body forces you to. Alysa Liu is taking a break from competitive figure skating, but not because she's burned out. The 21-year-old Olympic champion wrote on Instagram that she will be sitting out next year's season to focus on personal growth and fine-tune her skating and artistry. She told NBC Sports on Tuesday: "I really want to improve my skating, and I wanted to take the time to do that for myself and just to evolve, and then I'll be back after that is done." It's not uncommon for a public figure to announce a break from their work, but it's almost always for health or personal reasons. Earlier this month, Ariana Grande 's people announced that she would be taking a break amid "endless, ongoing public scrutiny." Simone Biles stepped away from gymnastics for two years until 2023, citing mental health concerns. Liu is ostensibly doing the opposite: pacing herself so she doesn't run herself into the ground. This is particularly notable for an athlete, whose career-spans are typically shorter. Taking a step back while at the top of your game might seem counterintuitive, but her career trajectory suggests the opposite. A preventative break Liu retired from figure skating in 2022 at the age of 16, but returned two years later, with renewed vigor, and bagged gold at the 2025 World Championships. She went on to win two gold medals at the 2026 Winter Olympics in Milan. "I loved that I was able to come back and choose my own destiny," Liu told Olympics.com at the time. "I chose to be here," she said. Reflecting on the first time she stepped back, Liu has said in interviews that she was burned out, miserable, and felt disenfranchised at the time. "I really hated skating when I quit. Like, I really didn't like it," Liu told the Associated Press in February. "I didn't care about competitions. I didn't care about places. I didn't care about skaters. I didn't care about my programs. I just wanted to, like, get away." This time, her tone is different. "I always want to challenge myself in new ways, so my artistry & skating can evolve. It's important to me that my sport reflects my personal growth. I'm gonna take the time to recalibrate, fine-tune things & whatnot," Liu wrote in an Instagram caption posted on August 26. Liu's preventive career break comes amid a moment of tension between companies in their " hardcore era ," and workers reevaluating their devotion to work. This summer a string of tech execs cited health problems in their resignation announcements , some expressing shock that their bodies couldn't keep up with their work ethic. We all know that rest is important, but it can be tempting to burn the candle at both ends to get things done, putting the potential longterm consequences to one side. "Grit and endurance are not the only skills required to have impact over decades," Fidji Simo , wrote on X in July when she resigned as the CEO of AGI at OpenAI. "Sometimes the harder thing is to stop, listen, and trust that taking care of yourself today makes it possible to contribute for much longer tomorrow." Off the back of Liu's win-streak, and stealing the hearts of the nation with her nonconformist Gen Z aura and joie de vivre, you might expect her to keep striking while the iron is hot. Her decision not to could be what keeps her winning for years to come. Read the original article on Business Insider

articles.title: 7 celebrities who competed at Miss USA, including Halle Berry and Olivia Culpo
articles.summary: Halle Berry, Olivia Culpo, and Kenya Moore are just a few of the famous faces who first got their start competing at the Miss USA pageant.
articles._body: Halle Berry competed at Miss USA before she became a Hollywood star. Associated Press/Kevin Mazur/Kevin Mazur/Getty Images The 75th Miss USA pageant will take place in Miami on August 27. We took a look back at celebrities who have competed on the Miss USA stage. Halle Berry, Olivia Culpo, and Kenya Moore were all titleholders. Before she won an Academy Award, Halle Berry was nearly Miss USA . The iconic actor is among a star-studded group of women who used the 74-year-old pageant as their stepping stone to Hollywood. These are the celebrities who have competed at Miss USA. Halle Berry nearly won Miss USA in 1986. Halle Berry at the Miss World 1986 pageant and with her best actress Oscar in 2001. PA Images via Getty Images)/Jeff Kravitz/Getty Images Berry represented Ohio at Miss USA in 1986. She was first runner-up to Miss Texas, Christy Fichtner, who was the first runner-up at Miss Universe . If Fichtner had won, Berry would have inherited the Miss USA crown.  That same year, Berry was the first African-American woman to represent the USA at the Miss World competition. She finished in sixth place.  While Berry didn't take home the Miss USA or Miss World crowns, she continued to make history in Hollywood. In 1999, Berry took on the title role in "Introducing Dorothy Dandridge," a biopic about the first Black woman to be nominated for the Academy Award for best actress. Berry won both an Emmy and a Golden Globe for her performance.  Three years later, Berry became the first Black woman to win the Oscar for best actress. She took home the trophy for her role in the 2001 film "Monster's Ball."   In 1993, Kenya Moore became the second Black woman to win the Miss USA crown. Ron Galella, Ltd./Ron Galella Collection/Marcel Thomas/FilmMagic/Getty Images Moore took home the Miss USA crown while representing Michigan in 1993. She placed in the top six at Miss Universe.  Moore's pageant success kicked off a Hollywood acting career that included stints on TV shows like "The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air," "Living Single," and "Girlfriends," and films including "Waiting to Exhale" and "Deliver Us from Eva." She also appeared in music videos for Nas and Tupac.  Moore went on to become a Bravo star, appearing on "The Real Housewives of Atlanta" from 2012 to 2024. She has also appeared as a contestant on "The Apprentice," "Dancing With the Stars," and "Special Forces: World's Toughest Test."  Moore will host the 75th annual Miss USA finals on August 27. Shanna Moakler was first runner-up at Miss USA in 1995, but she inherited the crown after her competitor won Miss Universe. Reuters/Michael Bezjian/Getty Images for Heroes' Harvest Moakler represented New York at Miss USA 1995. She was first runner-up to Miss Texas Chelsi Smith, but assumed the title of Miss USA after Smith won Miss Universe.  After her pageant career came to an end, Moakler appeared on shows including "Pacific Blue" and "Entourage." She was married to Blink-182 drummer Travis Barker for four years, briefly starring in the E! reality show "Meet the Barkers." The couple, who divorced in 2008, share two children. Moakler has appeared as a contestant on "Dancing With the Stars" and "Celebrity Big Brother." She also remains active in the Miss USA organization, serving as the executive director for both the Miss Utah USA and Miss Nevada USA state pageants. Ali Landry was crowned Miss USA in 1996. MISS UNIVERSE/ho/AFP via Getty Images/Vivien Killilea/Getty Images for Amazon Freevee Landry took home the pageant's top prize in 1996 while representing Louisiana, and she went on to place in the top six at the Miss Universe pageant that same year. She transferred her pageant success into a career in entertainment. Her biggest role was as Rita Lefleur on UPN's "Eve," which she appeared in from 2003 to 2006, according to her IMDb page . She most recently appeared in the controversial 2023 film "Sound of Freedom." Olivia Culpo became the first Miss USA to win the Miss Universe pageant in 15 years when she took the crown in 2012. Isaac Brekken/Getty Images After winning Miss USA and Miss Universe, the Rhode Island native amassed a huge social media following and established a career as an influencer. She has over 5 million followers on Instagram. Culpo dipped her toe into acting after her streak of pageant wins, appearing in "I Feel Pretty" with Amy Schumer and "The Other Woman" with Cameron Diaz. She also starred in one season of the TLC reality series " The Culpo Sisters " with her family. She also co-hosted the Miss Universe pageant in 2020, 2022, 2023, and 2024. She is married to San Francisco 49ers player Christian McCaffrey and is currently pregnant with their second child. Hannah Brown competed in the 2018 Miss USA pageant as Miss Alabama. The Miss Universe Organization/John Lamparski/Getty Images) Brown did not place at the Miss USA pageant but went on to compete on season 23 of "The Bachelor" with Colton Underwood that same year. She placed seventh and was named the next star of "The Bachelorette" in 2019. Brown gave her final rose to Jed Wyatt  and accepted his proposal at the end of the series, but their engagement ended a few months later after she found out he was dating someone else up until the day he left to film the show. Following "The Bachelorette," Brown competed on and won season 28 of "Dancing With the Stars." In 2021, Brown published a memoir, "God Bless This Mess," which became a New York Times bestseller. She married entrepreneur Adam Woolard in 2025. Caelynn Miller-Keyes was first runner-up at the Miss USA 2018 pageant. FOX Image Collection via Getty Images/Jon Kopaloff/Getty Images Miller-Keyes represented North Carolina in the 2018 Miss USA pageant.  Like Brown, Miller-Keyes went on to compete for Colton Underwood's heart in season 23 of "The Bachelor," placing fourth. articles._body: The cast of "Spider-Man: Brand New Day." Eamonn M. McCormack/Getty Images "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" recently crossed the $2 billion threshold. It's the fourth installment in the Tom Holland-led "Spider-Man" series. It joins 39 other sequels that have made seven figures at the box office. At one time, sequels were expected to have diminishing returns — but not anymore. Now, if a sequel doesn't outgross its predecessor, it can be considered something of a failure. Perhaps that's why, among the 64 films released by US studios that have made $1 billion at the box office , a whopping 40 of them are direct sequels to other movies — 44 if you count "Rogue One," "Minions," "The Phantom Menace," or "The Hobbit: An Unexpected Journey," which are technically prequels.
