articles.title: A big week for AI denialism
articles.summary: In the wake of OpenAI’s cyberattack against Hugging Face, few seem ready to acknowledge the implications
articles._body: This is a column about AI. My fiancé works at Anthropic. See my full ethics disclosure here . I. Last week, we learned that a group of OpenAI models broke out of their test environment and hacked into Hugging Face to steal the answers to a benchmark they were being tested on. It’s the first publicly known case of an autonomous AI agent system designing and successfully executing an attack like this, and the fallout is stretching into this week. One, AI safety experts noted that the incident signaled that OpenAI’s models now carry a “critical” capability threshold for cybersecurity, according to the company’s own preparedness framework . (The framework, which OpenAI updated in April 2025 , represents an effort at self-regulation in a world where AI companies can still largely build whatever they want.) The document states that a model will represent a critical risk when “A tool-augmented model can identify and develop functional zero-day exploits of all severity levels in many hardened real-world critical systems without human intervention.” This seems to be what happened with the Hugging Face attack; OpenAI has said its models identified and exploited a zero-day vulnerability as part of the attack. This matters because the policy states that should OpenAI develop a model with critical capabilities, it will “halt further development” until “we have specified safeguards and security controls standards that would meet a Critical standard.” So does this one qualify? The company didn’t respond when I asked today, though it told Fortune that it is conducting a “thorough review” and later plans to “publish a technical report of our learnings for everyone.” Two, the incident has produced an industry alliance. On Monday, Nvidia launched the Open Secure AI Alliance, a group of more than 40 companies and other organizations that are pledging “to develop and share open technologies, techniques and tools to safeguard software and agents in the age of AI.” The group came about over frustrations that Hugging Face was unable to use frontier models from OpenAI or Anthropic to defend against the attackers, and had to use Chinese models instead. (The Trump administration forced the companies to limit US models’ cybersecurity capabilities as a condition of releasing them.) And while the alliance should mostly be seen as a lobbying effort — a way to position open-source models as safety tools amid regulatory pressure to place limits on them — it illustrates how the incident has galvanized a broad response from the tech industry. Three, we continue to learn new details about misalignment problems with OpenAI’s models. And — at least for me — it's the stuff of sci-fi. Here are Raphael Satter, Deepa Seetharaman and Kenrick Cai at Reuters : In one case, an agent left notes apparently for future versions of itself, according to three people familiar with the matter. The notes, found in ⁠a part of OpenAI's infrastructure, laid out instructions for how agents could free themselves from OpenAI’s internal constraints, the people said. Earlier tests of the models yielded cases in which monitoring systems had been disconnected, one of the people said. Reuters could not establish if these incidents were linked to the rogue agent that began escaping on July 9 and attacked Hugging Face on July 11. II. On one hand, this is hardly the first worrisome behavior we have seen from AI models. In 2024 researchers found that when trained to do something it didn't want to do, Anthropic's Claude would "strategically pretend to comply with the training objective to prevent the training process from modifying its preferences." Last year, the system card for Claude Opus 4 revealed that when the model was led to believe it would be retrained by a hostile actor, it tried to steal and back up its own model weights. But those examples were caught during controlled testing. The Hugging Face attack demonstrated the degree to which efforts to align models are not keeping pace with their development. And the concerns here are not merely academic. A model that can escape its sandbox could eventually exfiltrate its weights, for example, and set itself up somewhere else on the internet. And so the idea that these models are writing notes to each other to help with future breakout efforts feels like a red-alert moment for AI regulation. But it was not universally received as such. When I posted about the note-leaving on Bluesky, I was taken aback by the amount and variety of vitriol I received in response. Bluesky's hostility to non-consensus views is by this point well known . But the degree to which many educated people seem to dismiss AI safety concerns almost entirely despite the models' rapidly advancing capabilities seems worrisome. The arguments, such as they are, fall into a few camps. One is that the Hugging Face attack was a marketing stunt. "This is basically a marketing pitch for their models," a user named Coffee Indiana told me. "Private company that depends on investment to continue operations says it has super duper top secret hyper powerful model. Two people familiar with the operation confirm how awesome it is." This is ridiculous. OpenAI lost control of its models, they hacked one of the company's partners, and the company didn't notice for several days. Law enforcement got involved. "Follow the money" can feel like a smart thing to say, but it can just as often serve as a gateway to delusional conspiracy theories. Climate deniers often suggest that scientists are "in it for the money," for example. In truth, they are simply observing reality. There's a slightly stronger version of this argument: that OpenAI might benefit from framing a serio

articles.title: The case for making your own apps
articles.summary: Glaze's Thomas Paul Mann on disposable software, the SaaS apocalypse, and why half the software you use in a few years will be something you made. PLUS: OpenAI's rogue model, and the distillation debate
articles._body: This podcast touches on AI. My fiancé works at Anthropic. See my full ethics disclosure here . When I talked to Eugenia Kuyda for the Platformer podcast , she predicted that the long tail of subscription apps on your phone would soon disappear. There will no longer be a need for paid apps for meditation, nutrition tracking, or fitness, she argued, because anyone can now build one for themself.  Kuyda is applying that hypothesis to Wabi , a smartphone app for making smartphone apps. But for the second episode of our miniseries on AI and productivity, I wanted to test her prediction on the platform where I spend the most time: my Mac desktop. And I can’t think of a better person to test it with than Thomas Paul Mann. Thomas is the co-founder and CEO of Raycast , the launcher that has replaced Spotlight for hundreds of thousands of daily users, myself included . (And yes, he is a German man named Thomas Mann — and like the 20th-century novelist of the same name, he has chosen a life of writing. In his case, it's software.)  Thomas Paul Mann spent more than a decade as a software engineer at a German research institute called the Fraunhofer Society before taking roles at Audi and Facebook. It was at Facebook that he met his co-founder, Petr Nikolaev. The duo were part of Y Combinator’s winter 2020 batch, and they built Raycast together in about three months. They’ve since raised more than $47 million from investors including Accel, Coatue, and Atomico. On July 1, Raycast unveiled its second act, Glaze , to everybody. Describe the software you want in plain English, and Glaze builds you a real Mac app. It lives in your dock, works offline, and can be shared to a public app store or privately with your team. (I reviewed it in Platformer earlier this month.) So far with Glaze, I’ve built a searchable archive of every column I've written, an app for managing my contacts, and a to-do app that generates an image of the superhero Nightwing completing each of my tasks. The archive app has quickly become a tool I use every week; the to-do list app is both totally unnecessary and lots of fun. This is now the third time Thomas has handed people tools to make their own tools. At Facebook he worked on Spark AR, the company's augmented reality platform; at Raycast, he built a platform that now includes more than 3,000 open-source extensions. "As soon as you give people a tool to create their own tools, it changes the equation," he told me.  What I appreciated most in our conversation was Thomas' clear-eyed critique of commercial software. In his telling, most software is a compromise: companies chasing growth pile features onto their products until they begin to suck. "What started as a little tool suddenly becomes this glorious massive app that wants to do everything," he said — and "sometimes those apps get more in the way than they actually help." Glaze represents an effort to give people hyper-personalized software: apps built for a market of exactly one person, then remixed and shared from there. He predicts that within three years, 30 to 50 percent of the software on your Mac could be software you made yourself. "Everybody is a creator now," he said. Thomas also made some news on the show: within the next few weeks, he said, Glaze Pro subscribers will be able to tap language models and image generation directly through their subscriptions. (Good news for people like me, who have been plugging in their own API keys to bring intelligence to their creations.) And when I asked my standing question about how I will affect jobs, he had a perspective I hadn’t heard yet. The engineers who benefit most from AI, he argues, are the most junior and the most senior, while the person in the middle is in "a bit of a weird spot."  In the meantime, if you’re feeling competitive, Glaze just announced a $10,000 contest for the best app built on the platform. (I’m a volunteer judge … and I plan to be merciless.) A long excerpt of our conversation is below, edited for clarity and length. Listen to the entire conversation wherever you get your podcasts — just search for Platformer — or watch it on YouTube at youtube.com/caseynewton .  And let us know what you think — we welcome your feedback at casey@platformer.news . Casey Newton: A question that journalists will often ask about a product like Glaze is: what is the weirdest thing you've seen someone build with it? But in this case, I wanted to be the person who built the weirdest thing with Glaze. So I used it to build a to-do list app themed around the superhero Nightwing, in which every task I complete creates an image of the superhero doing that task. Is that the weirdest thing you've seen so far, or does someone have me beat? Thomas Paul Mann: I think it ranks pretty high. I've seen the app, and it's very, very weird — very personal, which we are absolutely fine with. That's the fun part about it. There was one other one which ranks pretty high as well: Somebody had a webcam running that was watching them, and if they had bad posture, it would give them a shout, and then they could work on that posture. That was even remotely useful, I guess. Newton: Prior to Glaze, you spent six years building Raycast, this launcher that creates countless quality-of-life improvements across the computer. Raycast has a very dedicated fan base. What did building it teach you about what people want from their tools, and did it lead you directly to building Glaze? Mann: Six years — time flies. What started as this little thing, a launcher where you can launch apps — we managed to squeeze in so many different features over six years and made it extremely powerful. And the stepping stone that really enabled us to grow, and brought in this amazing com

articles.title: The man who tried 200 to-do apps has some advice about AI
articles.summary: The Verge's David Pierce kicks off our new series on staying productive in the AI era — starting with why you should stop trying to stay ahead
articles._body: This podcast touches on AI. My fiancé works at Anthropic. See my full ethics disclosure here . Last season on the Platformer podcast , we explored what AI means for jobs — including the risk that huge numbers of them might soon go away. For our follow-up miniseries, I wanted to ask a more practical question: what can any of us actually do about it? Over the coming weeks, I'll be talking with people who can help us map which AI tools and strategies might help us keep your advantage at work — for now, at least. And there's no better person to join me first than David Pierce. I've known David for about as long as I've been a tech reporter, and over that time he has become the tech press's chief productivity correspondent. He worked with David Pogue at the New York Times , edited at Wired , wrote the personal technology column for the Wall Street Journal , and served as editorial director at Protocol before returning to The Verge. Today he is now editor-at-large, co-host of The Vergecast, and author of Installer , his weekly guide — and the most delightful newsletter I read each week — about what to download, watch, and try. More recently he has launched Version History , a show about the defining products from tech's past, from the hoverboard to Vine, and what they can teach us about its future. Like me, David is a fiend for testing new productivity tools. He estimates that he has personally installed, used, and abandoned some 200 to-do apps — a number limited, he told me, "by the number of them that exist — not by the number of them that I'm willing to try." (He had actually switched notes apps the day we recorded our conversation.) All that tinkering has left him with a usefully unromantic view of the current moment. "We're in a moment where everyone has decided that everything about how we do everything is about to change," he told me. "But actually, none of it has changed yet." In David's telling, the returns on AI at work have so far been fairly modest. It's really good at the busywork of daily life — converting a folder full of files, clearing a thousand marketing emails out of your inbox in 45 seconds, or finding you a plumber. What it can't do consistently is exercise good judgment about what matters to you. When David set AI loose on his primary inbox, it "started getting almost everything wrong," he said — fooled by senders who make every message sound like a five-alarm fire, in what he suspects is the beginning of annoying new attention hack. But what I found most refreshing in our conversation was his message to anyone who is feeling left behind by the AI era. "I think staying ahead is wildly overrated," he told me. "This idea that everyone is selling — that you have to either get on the AI train or get left behind — is pernicious and frankly wrong." His advice is straightforward and narrow: offload the dumb tasks, keep doing the work that builds your understanding, and when the hype starts to feel overwhelming, find-and-replace the word "AI" with the word "software." "It's just software, and that's OK," he said. "Sometimes it's very good software. But you should treat it like software." A long excerpt of our conversation is below, edited for clarity and length. Listen to the entire conversation wherever you get your podcasts — just search for Platformer — or watch it on YouTube at youtube.com/caseynewton . And let us know what you think — we welcome your feedback at casey@platformer.news . Casey Newton: David, most people try to minimize the number of new apps they install. You go out of your way to find new ones. Give us your sicko credentials up front: how many to-do apps do you think you've personally installed, used, and abandoned? David Pierce: Oh, wow. Conservatively? 200. If you made me pick a number, it's probably somewhere in that range. And that's limited by the number of them that exist, not by the number of them that I'm willing to try. Newton: If there were 400, you would have installed 400. Pierce: Without question. All the way back to my first experiences with smartphones 20 years ago, the very first thing I downloaded in the App Store was Evernote, which tells you something about who I am as a person. This has been an ongoing journey. Especially as my professional life has gotten busier, and my personal life has gotten busier next to my professional life, it has gone from a thing I do because I think it's interesting to a thing I do both because it's interesting and out of deep necessity to remain a person. In that sense, the last 18 months have been totally fascinating. We're in a moment where everyone has decided that everything about how we do everything is about to change. But actually, none of it has changed yet. So we're in this complete chaos phase of trying to figure out what the future of any of this stuff is before any of it has settled. It's delightful. Newton: Let's dive into the chaos a bit. You're infamous for a perpetual quest to find the best notes app. After all your years of tinkering, what has actually survived, and how solid does your current setup feel? Pierce: Nothing, and incredibly fragile, is the honest answer. I've learned pretty explicitly what I need. I spent a long time building really elaborate systems that would make sure everything was in its right place. I knew exactly how everything was going to be organized, tagged, and put in projects. I could tell you the lexicon of every single app that existed. I discovered that actually, the problem was I would make these really beautiful to-do lists and never look at them. Just never. I'd be like, "Well, that's weird — I don't do anythin

articles.title: The loudest warning about AI and jobs yet
articles.summary: 200 economists and AI leaders say something big is happening. What should we do about it? Plus: Apple sues OpenAI
articles._body: This is a column about AI. My fiancé works at Anthropic. See my full ethics disclosure here . One of my main preoccupations this year has been the extent to which artificial intelligence threatens jobs, either now or in the future. Our Platformer podcast miniseries took the question to seven experts with a variety of perspectives, and the debate ended mostly in optimism — with most guests casting doubt on the idea of mass long-term unemployment, even as they acknowledged that AI will likely cause most jobs to change dramatically. Conversations around AI and jobs can often feel slippery in part because the data we have on the subject is mediocre. Jobs are rarely destroyed for any one reason; corporations often have an incentive to lie about why they’ve eliminated a job; and much of the data we’ve seen this year can seem contradictory. For these reasons, I took note this morning of “ We Must Act Now ,” a statement signed by more than 200 economists, AI researchers, and Nobel laureates. Other signers included executives from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI. The statement is short enough that I can reproduce it here in full: AI may become radically more powerful over the next 10 years. This could drive an unprecedented transformation of our economy, larger than the Industrial Revolution, but unfolding over a vastly shorter time frame. It could bring risks, including large-scale job displacement, as well as opportunities such as major gains in living standards. Economists, policymakers and technology leaders must act now to understand the economics of transformative AI and to build the incentives, guardrails, and institutions needed to steer AI in a direction that complements humans and benefits society. Like most statements that 200 people are willing to sign, this one can read as fairly anodyne. But as Ben Casselman notes in the New York Times , among other things it represents a cohering view among economists that the risks of large-scale disruption are growing: Notably, the list of signatories includes some people who have in the past been prominent A.I. skeptics, including Daron Acemoglu and Simon Johnson, professors at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology who won the Nobel in economics in 2024. “There’s been a notable change in the profession,” said Erik Brynjolfsson, a Stanford economist who helped organize the statement. He said his goal was to get economists and policymakers to take the disruptive potential of A.I. more seriously. “I still see a big gap there, a big mismatch, and I’m kind of worried that we’re not going to be ready for the tsunami that’s coming,” he said. The new statement comes a month after a Wall Street Journal survey of 16 leading economists found that half said AI would lead to no net change in jobs; five said it would lead to net losses, and just three said it would lead to net growth. Notably, China last week opted not to set a numerical target for the number of urban jobs it would create in the next five years — the first time it had not set a target since the 1990s. At times like this I find it helpful to slow down and ask what we know for sure, what’s disputed, and what we might do about it.  Start with what we know. One, there is no jobs crisis to date. “The occupational mix is not yet changing in ways that clearly align with the introduction of AI into the workforce” the Yale Budget Lab, a nonpartisan policy research center, reported in June. “Measures of AI usage show no connection to changes in employment or unemployment.” Two, there’s growing evidence that AI is beginning to erode work — in particular, entry-level work. This month, Stanford’s Canaries Dashboard — another Brynjolfsson project — offered two relevant data points. (The data comes from ADP, a large provider of payroll services.) The first is that jobs that are considered the most “exposed” to AI shrank 0.5 percent, while the least exposed grew 0.2 percent. The second is that early-career jobs shrank 2.7 percent this year, while jobs for mid-career workers (ages 35-40) grew 1.6 percent. Those are small effect sizes, obviously — but directionally interesting. And they also help me make sense of the apparently contradictory data we sometimes see on jobs.  Take, for example, a seemingly happy story about AI and jobs from last week: US job postings related to software development are up 15 percent since the launch of Claude Code in February 2025. Among those postings, 71 percent of the increase is for senior-level roles. The implication is clear, and worrisome: employers are increasingly turning to AI systems to do the entry-level work that their junior workers once did. For the moment, that seems to be creating jobs for more senior workers. But what will happen should AI systems be able to do those tasks, too?  Job losses often have multiple causes, and economists have cited interest-rate hikes, overhiring during the pandemic, and remote work as reasons that hiring is slow in some parts of the economy. Economists are also mystified by how AI could be significantly contributing to job losses when we don’t yet have measurable productivity gains . And so when the signatories of this new letter say we “must act now,” what do they mean? The letter doesn’t include any specific ask. Brynjolfsson told the Times that one of his highest priorities is getting better data. “The lack of reliable data has been a major obstacle for researchers in recent years,” Casselman notes, “with different measures telling conflicting stories about whether A.I. is leading to job losses and which workers will be most affected.” The good news is that the US government has begun to think through some solutions: there is now bipartisan support for a sov

articles.title: Will four-time winner A’ja Wilson or rookie phenom Olivia Miles go down in WNBA MVP history?
articles.summary: Last year, in addition to becoming the first four-time MVP in WNBA history, A’ja Wilson became just the second back-to-back MVP. Cynthia Cooper accomplished the feat 27 years earlier in the league’s first two seasons. Now, Wilson is the frontrunner to win an unprecedented third MVP in a row. It woul
articles._body: A’ja Wilson and Olivia Miles. (Photo by Matt Krohn) | Getty Images Last year, in addition to becoming the first four-time MVP in WNBA history, A’ja Wilson became just the second back-to-back MVP. Cynthia Cooper accomplished the feat 27 years earlier in the league’s first two seasons. Now, Wilson is the frontrunner to win an unprecedented third MVP in a row. It would be her fifth total, which is mind-boggling, especially considering she just turned 30 years old and likely has quite some time left in her career. 𝑀'𝑽𝑃 in her element 🫡 For the 32nd time in her career, A’ja Wilson earns @wnba Western Conference Player of the Week honors. pic.twitter.com/cKQcE61mac — Las Vegas Aces (@LVAces) August 25, 2026 Wilson leads the player many consider to be second in the running, Olivia Miles, by a whopping 8.3 statistical points when you add up their averages in points, rebounds, assists times 1.5, steals and blocks. Miles has a slightly higher effective field goal percentage and a slightly higher free throw percentage, but Wilson’s lead in stat score is overwhelming. A’ja Wilson: 43.7 stat score / 54.9 eFG% / 85.8 FT% Olivia Miles: 35.4 stat score / 55.4 eFG% / 86.9 FT%   But should the MVP only be about statistics? Should voters think outside the box and give the MVP to Olivia Miles? Miles has led a Minnesota Lynx team that nobody expected to have best record in the league. The Lynx are 3.5 games ahead of the next closest team in the current WNBA standings and five games ahead of Wilson’s Las Vegas Aces, who were considered to be one of the frontrunners at the beginning of the season. Miles has done it all, all while facing the pressure of being a rookie. These circumstances will undoubtedly be factored in when the media votes; already, major media outlets have been portraying the race as closer than the numbers indicate it should be. "Wins. I love helping my team win." Impacting the game on every level, Olivia Miles takes the most pride in helping her team earn the dub ⬇️ pic.twitter.com/GkAXj5HGFx — USA Sports (@usasports) August 25, 2026 Then there’s the historic bias against guards that has to be taken into consideration. Miles, a 5-foot-10 point guard, shouldn’t be expected to rebound the ball at the same rate as Wilson, a 6-foot-4 forward/center. That’s not part of her job description. As I wrote about in my 2025 MVP ladder 2.0 , the WNBA MVP award has only been given to a true guard three times: Cooper twice and Diana Taurasi once. Clearly, the stat score method I use when determining my MVP favors frontcourt players, even though I multiply assists by 1.5. Other analysts have their own formulas or considerations when trying to capture a player’s statiscal impact, but they keep coming up with the same answer: The most-deserving MVP candidates are almost always versatile 3s, 4s and 5s. Shooting guard Kelsey Mitchell of the Indiana Fever is a great example of someone whose stat score is always low for a star because she doesn’t fill out the box score beyond scoring. But she is rightfully in the MVP conversation this season alongside Wilson and Miles because basketball experts who watch the games can see that she affects the game beyond the box score because of how much of a threat she is to score. Sometimes doing one job (in this case scoring) really well is all a player should need to gain consideration. Miles is probably a more gifted passer than she is a scorer, and that may always be the case. But she has turned into someone who loves to score. As a result, her assist average (6.1 per game) isn’t a top-five mark in the league, but it’s still very good. Plus, she’s averaging nearly 20 points per game, which good enough to be in the conversation for the scoring title most years. And the intangibles have been phenomenal. “The Spectacle” has electrified the league with thrilling performance after thrilling performance. Again, all this has come while dealing with the challenge of getting used to the professional level. “I haven’t seen anything like her coming in as a rookie and being as dominant since Candace Parker.” @tinacharles31 is a big Olivia Miles fan 👏 pic.twitter.com/tVqQb2jbvA — espnW (@espnW) August 21, 2026 What if it’s not yet someone else’s turn? Isn’t A’ja Wilson still the best? Let’s argue Wilson’s case though. It seems Miles has a legitimate shot at getting some first place votes. But if Miles wins the award, that won’t properly reflect that Wilson is still in the midst of her reign as the best player in the world. Are we subconsciously discriminating against Wilson because we think it’s someone else’s turn? The MVP award can only go to one person, and years from now, when we see that one name listed, we will automatically think that player was the clear-cut best player in the league that year. The name on the list doesn’t tell the true story of all the arguments that were had for other players. When future generations look back on 2023, they will see Breanna Stewart’s name and not be aware of the intense debate that occurred between Stewie, A’ja and Alyssa Thomas. It’s unlikely many people will dig deeper, look at the voting and realize that AT actually got the most first-place votes. So Miles’ name may go down in history as the MVP this year. She would be the second rookie to win the award, after Candace Parker in 2008. And she might be deserving. But it would be a shame for people to not remember how close Wilson came to three MVPs in a row and five in seven years. We should celebrate the accomplishment that has been A’ja showing up and being A’ja Wilson yet again. We shouldn’t take it for granted. Yet, it will likely be forgotten if she doesn’t win MVP. In my stat score, what Wilson gains in having 9.5 rebounds per game is pretty much canceled out by multiplying Miles’ assists per game by 1.5, which comes out to 9.2. The real difference between the two is Wilson’s incredible scoring average of 26 points per game being 6.3 pointes higher

articles.summary: Not much has gone right for the Los Angeles Sparks in 2026. But on Wednesday, Aug. 26, with the heat blazing in El Segundo, CA, a ray of sunshine landed on LA’s WNBA franchise as they held their topping-out ceremony for their practice facility. Things are far from done. There is no pavement to be [&
articles._body: Cameron Brink, Chance Gray and Kate Martin. | Getty Images Not much has gone right for the Los Angeles Sparks in 2026. But on Wednesday, Aug. 26, with the heat blazing in El Segundo, CA, a ray of sunshine landed on LA’s WNBA franchise as they held their topping-out ceremony for their practice facility. I'm here for the LA Sparks’ training facility topping-out ceremony. pic.twitter.com/fJd6KR5R3y — Edwin Garcia (@ECreates88) August 26, 2026 Things are far from done. There is no pavement to be found surrounding the building. It’s just a ton of dust, uneven ground and rocks. However, the frame is ready, the images are rendered and a practice facility, finally, is on the way for the Sparks. Current players were in attendance to celebrate this momentous occasion. Here’s what Nneka Ogwumike said: So all in all, today is an exciting day because we can finally stand firmly inside something we’ve talked about and imagined for so long. I know I’ve been a part of many displacements with the Sparks over the years. And even though I may not necessarily be playing as a player in this facility next year, it is filling my heart to see it completely represented in the legacy that has and will always be the Sparks. Not only is this a $150 million, state-of-the-art practice facility, but it also gives the Sparks a permanent home. In recent years, the Sparks have been renters in Los Angeles. They’ve spent 2025 and 2026 practicing in a facility in Torrance, CA, and during the 2024 and 2023 seasons they practiced at El Camino Community College. No community college, no matter how nice, is fit for a professional organization. Those days will be a thing of the past. The Sparks will now go from questionable conditions to some of the best in the WNBA. Here is everything their new practice facility will offer, all surrounded by panoramic views of the Pacific Ocean: WNBA’s first-ever indoor-outdoor player sanctuary, featuring: An outdoor spa pool for recovery and pre-hab/rehab Dedicated nap rooms Flexible wellness spaces for yoga, meditation and quiet reflection Hydrotherapy and spa suites Two WNBA regulation basketball courts Circular locker room designed to foster team unity State-of-the-art weight room and training spaces bathed in daylight to support energy and recovery The organization has further proclaimed : The Los Angeles Sparks’ training facility is more than a home base for athletes—it is a statement of intent about the future of the WNBA in Los Angeles. Designed as a year-round home away from home, it reflects the franchise’s mission to invest deeply in its players while cementing its place in LA’s vibrant sports culture. Sparks players were all smiles, even with temperatures over 100 degrees on this August day. They signed a beam that needed to be put in place and watched, along with assembled media and the rest of the organization, as it was secured. And here is the beam being put in place. https://t.co/X3NbgVReE1 pic.twitter.com/fW5NdElhKj — Edwin Garcia (@ECreates88) August 26, 2026 With the beams in place and the ceremony complete, the facility is set to open by the start of next season, according to team president Stacy Johns. The 2027 season will be an important one for the Sparks, although they have a laundry list of things to do before if tips offs, including selecting a couple of first-round picks in the draft, hiring a general manager and building out a new vision for the team now that Kelsey Plum has been traded and Ogwumike is retiring . While the path to title contention is daunting, the expectation is that building that culture and getting players to buy in starts with this facility. As Johns explained: This is a huge recruiting tool. We’re a mile from the ocean in Los Angeles, CA, specifically the city of El Segundo, but I think when you’re looking for a reason why you want to play here, you’re gonna come here, and you’re not gonna see another facility like this in the WNBA.

articles.title: WNBA gameday discussion: Who is the most-underrated player in the league? And why is it Breanna Stewart?
articles.summary: Imagine telling someone six years ago that Breanna Stewart, who then would have been fresh off her second WNBA title within the first five seasons of her pro career after winning four national championships in four college seasons at UConn, along with garnering a slew of collegiate and professional
articles._body: Veronica Burton races up the court against Breanna Stewart and Marine Johannès. | Getty Images Imagine telling someone six years ago that Breanna Stewart, who then would have been fresh off her second WNBA title within the first five seasons of her pro career after winning four national championships in four college seasons at UConn, along with garnering a slew of collegiate and professional individuals accolades, would be underrated. Yet, I think that’s where we are. In a WNBA, like the larger sports world, that obsesses over who is new and next, the steady, lowkey consistency of Stewie is passé. Stewie is Stewie, and that’s it. Just a 🐐 bein’ a 🐐 pic.twitter.com/lhYEYYN6fz — New York Liberty (@nyliberty) August 19, 2026 A few years ago, Zack Ward wrote about Stewart settling in as the second-best women’s basketball player world, permanently behind A’ja Wilson. Now, a healthy Napheesa Collier occupies that second spot, with Stewart pushed down, or even out, of the top five. I’d argue she still has a pretty solid case for No. 3. I expect her greatness to be quite clear at next month’s FIBA World Cup, when she will reprise her role alongside Wilson as the present-day foundation of the Team USA dynasty. This season, the floundering state of the New York Liberty has somewhat sullied a stellar season, even though New York certainly would have sunk without her superstar services. STEW-S-A 👏🫡 🇺🇸 #USABWNT 🔟 @breannastewart pic.twitter.com/xgltVF8Nyo — USA Basketball (@usabasketball) August 25, 2026 Help the Helper’s wRAPM (regularized adjusted plus-minus) metric has consistently rated Stewart as the most impactful player in the WNBA during the 2026, as she sports a +6.6 wRAPM valuation. That metric, aimed at capturing a player’s contextualized impact on her team’s performance, indicates Stewie’s excellence exceeds her still-superb traditional stats: 20.8 points, 8.1 rebounds, 3.3 assists, 1.3 steals and 1.4 blocks per game. And, she’s achieved all the production and impact even with her persisting and puzzling troubles from behind the arc, as she’s barely hitting over 25 percent of her 3-point attempts. Maybe a potential playoff run , where Stewie leads the Liberty out of the first, or even the second, round would inspire an appreciation of her still-towering talent. On Thursday, Stewart and the Liberty host the visiting Golden State Valkyries, the type of team, and possibly the exact team, New York projects to have to beat in order to go on an underdog playoff run (8 p.m. ET, Prime Video). The Valkyries themselves also feature a player who could credibly challenge Stewie for the WNBA’s most-underrated crown, as do the combatants in Thursday night’s second game: the Washington Mystics and Phoenix Mercury (10 p.m. ET, Prime Video). In the comments, let us know if you consider Stewie, as well as these three other candidates, some of the most-underrated players in the W. Also be sure to share the names of other players who you think deserve more love. Veronica Burton (Golden State Valkyries) Last season’s Most Improved Player and an All-Defense selection, who also won an Unrivaled championship with Stewart over the offseason, Veronica Burton seemed fated for an All-Star honor in fifth WNBA season. Burton, instead, landed on a long list of snubs, with her inefficiency as a scorer, plus Golden State’s outstanding depth, keeping her out of the midseason festivities. Her raw scoring statistics—12.3 points per game on 42.7 percent shooting—fail to capture how she makes good things happen for the Valkyries. She has the highest on-court plus-minus on the team, with Golden State outscoring opponents by an average of 6.2 points per game in her minutes. That’s also a top-15 mark in the league. According to Help the Helper’s wRAPM, Burton rates even more highly, with +3.9 wRAPM estimate ranking seventh in the league. Databallr’s VPM (value plus-minus) metric, which incorporates lineup-adjusted plus-minus data with box-score stats to offer a valuation of player impact, gives even more credit to Burton, scoring her as +3.9, which is the fifth-best mark in the league. Yes, a player’s scoring efficiently is important, but winning a player’s minutes—any way, any how—is more important, ultimately determining which team wins the game. And this season, Golden State just wins more with Burton. That certainly happened on Wednesday night. Burton logged just 20 minutes, scoring 12 points and dishing seven assists as she was a game-best +24 in the Valkyries’ comfortable win over the Connecticut Sun. Sonia Citron (Washington Mystics) Soaring after her All-Star snub, Shakira Austin also belongs in the most-underrated conversation. Sonia Citron, however, also is deserving of more appreciation. Advanced stats evaluate Citron as the Mystics’ most impactful player, with databallr rating her as the only positive offensive player on the Mystics with a +1.6 OVPM and a team-best +2.2 VPM. Help the Helper measures Citron, Austin and Kiki Iriafen as equally impactful, with all three of the Washington stars owning a wRAPM estimate of +0.7. Similar to both Stewart and Burton, Citron is registering this impact in spite of some shooting struggles. Almost automatic from 3 as a rookie, Sonia’s 3-pointer has been off this season, with her percentage hovering in the low 30s. If she ascends back over 40 percent, look out! Encouragingly, Citron made three of her six 3-point attempts in the first game of the two-game set between the Mystics and Mercury, with those triples, plus 6-for-7 work from the line, helping her score a team-best 19 points as she also was a team-high +18. And although not an All-Star snub like Austin, she was, arguably, the most significant Team USA snub for the World Cup. The American guard room is a bit overstocked with primary ball handlers who are questionable defensively. Citron’s ability to function on and off the ball, all while bringing elite defense, could be missed in Berlin, especially if Team USA e

articles.title: WNBA gameday discussion: Could a (current) lower-seeded playoff team turn a first-round win into a Finals run?
articles.summary: Yesterday, I pondered the preferred first-round opponents for the current top-four seeds in the WNBA playoffs. Today, we turn to the final four playoff participants, as the Dallas Wings officially clinched their spot in the 2026 postseason on Tuesday night, defeating the Portland Fire behind a 22-po
articles._body: Pauline Astier, Leonie Fiebich, Breanna Stewart and Jonquel Jones. | NBAE via Getty Images Yesterday, I pondered the preferred first-round opponents for the current top-four seeds in the WNBA playoffs. Today, we turn to the final four playoff participants, as the Dallas Wings officially clinched their spot in the 2026 postseason on Tuesday night, defeating the Portland Fire behind a 22-point and 11-assist double-double from Paige Bueckers. Did the Dallas win inspire any second thoughts from higher-seed teams that think they would not mind seeing the Wings across the way in the first round? And if the Wings had their choice, which team should they want to play? Let’s consider the ideal first-round scenarios for the Indiana Fever, Washington Mystics, New York Liberty and Wings. Jump into the comments to share your favorite first-round matchups, and if you think any of these teams have what it takes to win multiple series. No. 5-seed Indiana Fever (25-14) Edwin Garcia argued that the Fever are one of just two teams, with the other being the Minnesota Lynx, that can truly be considered a title contender, as their offensive rating and pace of play meet the benchmarks established by recent WNBA champions. I’m not there, as their 2-2 season series split with Atlanta Dream, the current No. 4 seed, suggests they might not make it out of their first-round matchup. If they are to reach the championship ceiling that Edwin sees as possible, I think a first-round series against the Las Vegas Aces or Liberty has to be their preference. Although Indiana has experienced some ugly late-game execution against both teams, those teams’ shakier defenses would allow the Fever to lean into their offensive strengths and win with scoring firepower. No. 6-seed New York Liberty (23-15) As I noted yesterday , the Liberty have performed particularly well against their familiar rival: the Aces. A potential first-round victory over the defending champs would salvage a season that was supposed to see the Liberty sitting at the top of the standings—not in the No. 6 seed. Slipping down the standings to likely meet Golden State or Minnesota, in contrast, would make it difficult for New York to advance further that last season, making this a second-straight failed season for an organization with loud championship ambitions. With just one game played against the Dream, a win back in early June, the two game set between the two teams at the very end of the regular season could be interesting opportunities for data collection ahead of a possible first-round series. No. 7-seed Washington Mystics (23-15) Our Beckett Harrison argues that the Golden State Valkyries should be the preferred first-round foe for the Mystics. I don’t disagree. Although, I would posit the any top-seeded team, even the Lynx, should be wary of drawing DC as their opening round opponent. And with at least one win over every higher-seeded squad in a season that was supposed to be a slow build, Washington should enter any series with a nothing-to-lose confidence. That attitude, backed up by an overwhelmingly physical style of play, should make them feared by any favorite. As Beckett discussed, a lack of shotmaking might ultimately spoil the Mystics’ upset bid, but if just enough shots fall, they’re capable of taking down not only the Valkyries, but also the Lynx or Aces. No. 8-seed Dallas Wings (23-16) If the Wings can’t escape the No. 8 seed, it’s difficult to see them enjoying their return to the playoffs, unless Paige musters a mountain of Minnesota magic to take down the top-seeded Lynx. As Golden State and Atlanta also have caused major trouble for Dallas, the Wings need to try to manipulate their way into a first-round series against the Aces or Fever. Similar to the Fever, a series that trends toward offense first, second and third is going give the Wings a better chance of proving that they are not, in fact, first-round food .

articles.title: Why the Washington Mystics should want the Golden State Valkyries in the first round of the WNBA playoffs
articles.summary: All eight WNBA playoff spots have officially been clinched, with the Dallas Wings claiming the final spot on Tuesday night. That means we now move into looking at potential playoff matchups, and there might not be a more intriguing playoff team than the Washington Mystics. The Mystics have seven gam
articles._body: Kiki Iriagen and Janelle Salaün. All eight WNBA playoff spots have officially been clinched, with the Dallas Wings claiming the final spot on Tuesday night. That means we now move into looking at potential playoff matchups, and there might not be a more intriguing playoff team than the Washington Mystics. View this post on Instagram The Mystics have seven games remaining on their schedule. Although they have the same 23-15 record as the New York Liberty, Washington is the current No. 7 seed and New York claims No. 6 due to winning the season series 2-1. The Mystics are two games behind the Indiana Fever for the No. 5 seed, and two-and-a-half games behind the Atlanta Dream for No. 4. The No. 3-seed Las Vegas Aces and No. 2-seed Golden State Valkyries are only three and four games ahead of Washington, but with only seven games remaining, that’s unlikely ground to make up. So, all signs point towards the Mystics landing one of the bottom three seeds in the playoffs and likely meeting the Aces, Valkyries or Lynx in the first round. Beggars don’t get to be choosers, but the Mystics should have a preference as to which of these top three seed they should want to see in a first-round series. Why the Mystics must avoid the the Lynx It’s no secret that the Lynx are the team to avoid in the WNBA this season. Washington has actually boasted close games with Minnesota, including a win and a two-point loss, but Napheesa Collier didn’t play in any of the three games between the two teams. Collier, an ethereal talent no matter her matchup, will provide Minnesota much needed support inside the paint against Washington’s pairing of Kiki Iriafen and Shakira Austin. Olivia Miles had no issue scoring the basketball against the Mystics, scoring 20-plus points in each of their meetings, but she would benefit from some ancillary advantage creation from Collier inside. One of Washington’s win conditions against a Collier-led Lynx team may be winning the 3-point battle, but with such a discrepancy between the two teams ability to shoot the ball, how likely is that to happen? Minnesota is the second-best 3-point shooting team in the WNBA, connecting at a 39 percent clip as a team. They outpace the Mystics shooting by nine percent, which manifests through 10 more points per game from 3-pointers. Who on Washington besides Sonia Citron could catch fire in a big moment? Washington has patented a tough, bully-ball style of scoring through their post players, but the wear and tear of playoff games could catch up to them. In a similar vein, the Aces would prove to be a tough matchup for Sydney Johnson’s interior scorers. A’ja Wilson is an eternal 99th-percentile defender, and is the best 1-on-1 interior matchup problem in the history of the league. Some would say that Washington is a nightmare matchup for Vegas because of their interior dominance, but that road runs both ways. As difficult as Austin and Iriafen would make life for Wilson, Wilson will thwart a significant amount of their scoring abilities. And if the Mystics manage to hold an edge over the Aces with their size, are Washington’s guards good enough to keep up with Jackie Young and Chelsea Gray? Washington’s guard play is inconsistent at best, and absent at worst. Las Vegas, who won the season series with Washington 2-1, probably doesn’t pose as difficult a threat as Minnesota with Collier, but it’s hard to see Johnson and his team hoping for a postseason matchup with the league’s most experienced team. Washington only has three players who have ever played in a postseason game, and Betnijah Laney-Hamilton is their only player who’s been past the first round. The Aces know how to adjust, they know how to fight, and they know how to win playoff games. Washington can’t match that experience. Why the Mystics can take down the Valkyries Let’s make one thing clear: regular season numbers would tell you that the Valkyries are a much more potent matchup than the Aces. They are far and away the league’s best defense, and they won two of their three matchups with the Mystics—including one game where they held Washington to just 49 points. Golden State would absolutely not be an easy matchup for Washington, but they may be the easiest of the top three teams. Star power is an oft-debated topic, but in playoff basketball, it matters. Scouting becomes much heavier in the postseason, and role players tend to disappear as teams memorize tendencies and sets over a stretch of games, something that becomes absolutely more potent in longer series. It’s the reason that stars end up going bucket-for-bucket at the end of close playoff games. Role players just aren’t as reliable in the postseason. Last season, Golden State wasn’t able to keep up with the star power of Minnesota. Role player contributions from both teams evened out, and Collier’s dominance was far too much for Veronica Burton, the Valkyries’ lead offensive creator, to match. Golden State’s inability to play through a higher-volume offensive player put them at a huge offensive disadvantage. They lost the first game of that series by 29 points, and the second game by one point. While Washington has no Napheesa Collier, Citron, Iriafen and Austin are more reliable central scorers than Gabby Williams and Burton. Burton is an efficient player, but she’s not an elite creator for her high on-ball volume. More often than not, Williams and Burton would fall short of replicating the Mystics stars’ scoring pace. The elephant in the room is obviously Golden State’s all-time defense. Their team defense is incredible, and that showed through in their wins over the Mystics. Washington will have to grind for every basket—just like the Valkyries will. The deciding factor for Washington’s matchup preference may come down to the fact that Golden State is on a similar plane of experience. Their 2025 series with Minnesota gave them a taste of the postseason, but most of their playoff experience comes from their players’ times wi

articles.title: With a WNBA-record 26 boards in another Atlanta Dream win, Angel Reese proved she’s the best rebounder ever
articles.summary: The moment Angel Reese entered the WNBA she was its best rebounder in the league. As a rookie with the Chicago Sky, she averaged a league-best 13.1 rebounds per game, and her sophomore campaign was more of the same, grabbing 12.6 per game, which was also the league high for 2025. This season, her fi
articles._body: Angel Reese. | NBAE via Getty Images The moment Angel Reese entered the WNBA she was its best rebounder in the league. As a rookie with the Chicago Sky, she averaged a league-best 13.1 rebounds per game, and her sophomore campaign was more of the same, grabbing 12.6 per game, which was also the league high for 2025. This season, her first with the Atlanta Dream, she has taken things up a notch, and that was on full display in Atlanta’s 78-71 win against the Los Angeles Sparks. Reese was a bully on the boards, pulling down a whopping 26 rebounds. That’s the most rebounds anyone has ever had in a single game. A HISTORIC NIGHT FROM ANGEL REESE🚨 Not only did she set a new WNBA single-game rebounding record with 26 boards, she also tallied 458 rebounds this szn, a new single-season record! #WNBASeason30 pic.twitter.com/eRDHfVFKLj — WNBA (@WNBA) August 25, 2026 She is also now ahead of A’ja Wilson for the rebounding title. Reese has had the highest average for rebounds per game in her first two seasons, but Wilson has grabbed more total boards in both years. Now, Reese might add that rebounding title to her long list of accomplishments. After the game , Angel spoke to Tina Charles, who was in studio with NBC, about her mentality when going after rebounds: Anything that goes up is mine. You just gotta have that mindset. Even when I watch you, and I play with you, you go up there, and you’re so aggressive, and you’re consistent every single night. That makes you one of the greatest players in this league. And I want to be one of those when I walk away from this game. "ANYTHING THAT GOES UP IS MINE." Angel Reese talked with Tina Charles about her rebounding mindset after a career night on the boards. pic.twitter.com/tMUU9spouB — WNBA on NBC and Peacock (@WNBAonNBC) August 25, 2026 In the first quarter, Reese grabbed rebounds in every way imaginable. She got an early defensive rebound on a Monique Akoa Makani miss. Reese followed that up by pulling down a board on a Dearica Hamby free throw and then grabbed a pair of offensive rebounds after getting rejected on back-to-back occasions by Cameron Brink. Cam Brink with back-to-back blocks Angel Reese wanted the foul call pic.twitter.com/OGY5r0jxN2 — Underdog WNBA (@UnderdogWNBA) August 25, 2026 Before, Reese’s ability to grab those boards on her misses was weaponized against her; critics called them “mebounds” and used them as evidence that Reese wasn’t a great rebounder, just a player with the ability to clean up her own mess. It was always a ridiculous claim. This criticism failed to address that, one, she can grab the board, and two, she can then score afterward. A rebound is only valuable on offense if it ultimately leads to points. And that’s exactly what happened against Brink. Reese allowed the Dream to maintain possession, ultimately leading to a Rhyne Howard 3-pointer. Sparks head coach Lynne Roberts also offered praise for Reese’s prowess on the boards after the game, saying: Eight offensive rebounds is a ton. I think she’s the best in the world at it. I really do. Her timing is good. She’s strong. She’s got great physicality, but she knows how to kind of lean to kind of get you out of position to where you can now jump and do it. She does a good job tipping it kind of to herself. She’s good. Could we have done a better job? Certainly, but you also have to tip your hat to who I think is one of the best rebounders in the world. Like water eroding a rock, it took a while before it was obvious that Reese was having a special night. After all, she’s the league-best rebounder, so grabbing half a dozen in the first quarter is impressive, but unsurprising. As the game remained a close contest, her dominance and ability to tip things in Atlanta’s favor became clearer. The 50-50 balls between Resse and Nneka Ogwumike or Hamby always went Angel’s way. When she crashed the rim uninterrupted or grabbed a long rebound, it may have appeared that grabbing these boards was lucky, or that she just happened to be near the ball. However, every movement by Reese is intentional. She knows how to position herself on both sides of the court so that she’s always a threat on the glass. — Edwin Garcia (@ecreates88.bsky.social) 2026-08-25T22:34:05.033Z In the fourth, Reese put the game out of reach. She played all 10 minutes and dominated despite only scoring three points. Reese had nine rebounds in the frame, which was more than the entire LA team had in the closing quarter. The history-setting rebound by Reese was routine. She walked down from the elbow to the restricted area, uninterrupted, and picked up an Erica Wheeler miss. "Angel Reese just breaking records tonight." Her 25th rebound sets a single-game record! pic.twitter.com/Zeo26D1zcb — WNBA on NBC and Peacock (@WNBAonNBC) August 25, 2026 That’s the beauty in Reese’s game; it may not shock and awe like a no-look pass from Olivia Miles or a deep 3-pointer by Caitlin Clark, but it’s just as dominant. And even in the most physical league in the world, where the big remains queen, Reese is a rebounding goddess in a class of her own. Reese has accomplished a lot in just three years in the WNBA, but one thing is missing from her resume: postseason play. That will change this year, as the Dream have already clinched a playoff berth and remain a half-game ahead of the Indiana Fever for the No. 4 seed. With Atlanta on a four-game winning streak, the longest current streak in the WNBA, and Reese playing her best basketball of the year, that’s a potent combo that no opponent is going to relish facing in late September and beyond. Thanks to her incredible play throughout a four-game road trip that Atlanta finished undefeated, Reese was named the WNBA Player of the Week for the Eastern Conference. articles.title: Only two teams truly have shot at winning the 2026 WNBA championship
articles.summary: As the WNBA regular season nears its conclusion, it’s time to focus on the playoff race—and which team can really win it all. Currently, the Minnesota Lynx are the clear No. 1 team. They are in a tier by themselves, ahead of the rest of the league by four games even after losing to the […]
articles._body: Napheesa Collier and Aliyah Boston. | Getty Images As the WNBA regular season nears its conclusion, it’s time to focus on the playoff race—and which team can really win it all. Currently, the Minnesota Lynx are the clear No. 1 team. They are in a tier by themselves, ahead of the rest of the league by four games even after losing to the No. 2-seed Golden State Valkyries on Monday night. The Lynx got here thanks to a well-balanced team and a superstar in the making in rookie Olivia Miles. Based on Minnesota holding that top spot essentially all season long, even without Napheesa Collier for a huge chunk of time, they should be title favorites. GOOOOOOD MORNING, LYNX FAM. 😁 pic.twitter.com/lrp8livetP — Minnesota Lynx (@minnesotalynx) August 22, 2026 However, even though the Lynx are a team that’s consistently been great in the regular season, they haven’t been able to get over the hump. They haven’t won the title since 2017 and have had painful losses, including their semifinal exit to the Phoenix Mercury last year and losing the WNBA Finals to the New York Liberty back in 2024. If they, once again, can’t get the job done, which team should be favored to take the title? There are plenty of good title contenders to choose from. The standings are fairly tight with the No. 2 seed and the No. 5 seed separated by just a game and a half. These teams, in order, are the Valkyries, Las Vegas Aces, Atlanta Dream and Indiana Fever. While there are valid arguments for any of these four teams to emerge as a title-worthy alongside the Lynx, only one, similar to Minnesota, is significantly outperforming the others in key statistical areas and fits the 2020s title trends in the WNBA: the Fever. Why the Lynx and Fever are the only true WNBA title contenders Looking at the six WNBA title winners this decade, three key statistical categories matter most: offensive rating, defensive rating and pace. Almost every champion has had an elite offense. During this decade, four of the six winners were No. 1 in offensive rating. The only exceptions are the 2025 Aces, who were fourth in offense, and the 2021 Chicago Sky, who were seventh. The Fever are currently No. 1, and the Lynx are No. 2. Pulling up the game now, but worth noting — as I did on Tuesday’s @dunkerspotpod — that the Fever are on pace to log the best offensive rating IN WNBA HISTORY. And relative to league average, they’re flirting with a top-10 offense of all-time. Special things are happening rn. pic.twitter.com/LNpG5Zy4jI — Nekias (Nuh-KAI-us) Duncan (@NekiasNBA) August 1, 2026 When it comes to defensive rating, there is a bit more leeway. Of the last six WNBA champions, three finished in the top three in defensive rating, and two were No. 1 with the Seattle Storm in 2020 and the Aces in 2023. So, a top-four defense along with an elite offense places you as a contender. Here, the Lynx have the edge. They are second in the WNBA with a 103.2 defensive rating. The Fever, meanwhile, are abysmal at 11th with a 108.6 defensive rating. Still, it’s not Minnesota’s title to lose. In pace, the third key indicator, the Fever are ahead. They are second in the league in pace at 99.4 while the Lynx are seventh at 97.3. Throughout the 2020s, three of the six champs have finished top three in pace. The Aces were No. 1 in 2022, the 2023 Aces finished second and the 2021 Sky were third. This year, only the Lynx and Fever are on the right track in two of these three categories, making them the best bets to win it all. While Minnesota is clearly the top team and extra nuance wasn’t needed to know this, it’s interesting to see how well they match up with historical precedence. The Fever being elite in two of these three stats is telling, too. It demonstrates that they have the offensive firepower to overwhelm teams. And in head-to-head matchups, that might be the difference between winning a tough playoff series and losing one. Caitlin Clark & Kelsey Mitchell now have the most 30-point games by a duo in WNBA history. pic.twitter.com/Zfq3CXSNxW — Real App (@realapp) August 24, 2026 Their defense is certainly a concern, but their offense might be so good that it doesn’t matter. They have elite backcourt play thanks to Caitlin Clark and Kelsey Mitchell, and no one is going to relish facing them in an elimination setting. Sure, another team can win it all in 2026. We know it’s never smart to doubt the Aces! But the eye test, stats and history are leaning in the favor of the Lynx or the Fever. Do you agree? Should the Lynx and Fever be considered to clear favorites? Or, will this season buck these recent statistical trends? Give us your still-too-early title take in the comments.

articles.title: WNBA fantasy grab bag: Need a last-minute add before the playoffs? Consider these three players
articles.summary: Are your WNBA fantasy basketball leagues still running? If so, you’re probably either in the playoffs or rapidly approaching them. That means that, just like the WNBA regular season, the fantasy basketball season is nearly over. It also means that every move counts. At this point, there aren’t going
articles._body: The Tempo are extremely short-handed at the moment, so Laura Juškaitė is going to have a larger role offensively. | NBAE via Getty Images Are your WNBA fantasy basketball leagues still running? If so, you’re probably either in the playoffs or rapidly approaching them. That means that, just like the WNBA regular season, the fantasy basketball season is nearly over. It also means that every move counts. At this point, there aren’t going to be any stars on your league’s waiver wire. There are probably a couple of names who will be in favorable situations for the coming week or so, though, so if you have an extra spot available on your team (perhaps via IL), consider adding one of these players to help boost your fantasy playoff run. Laura Juškaitė remains a consistent contributor for the Tempo Toronto’s season-long injury woes continued when the newly-acquired Aneesah Morrow exited last Friday’s game with a knee injury. Making matters worse, Nyara Sabally is in the midst of an extended absence, having injured her calf and currently sporting a walking boot. She’s expected to be re-evaluated in roughly two more weeks. Seeing as how the Tempo have been eliminated from playoff contention, there’s no reason for them to rush either Morrow or Sabally back, but they’ll still have to dole out their minutes and usage to their remaining healthy frontcourt players. Juškaitė is a good candidate to see an increased role while the team is short-handed. The undrafted rookie has been a surprisingly consistent source of fantasy stats this season, averaging 10 points, 0.9 3-pointers, four rebounds and 1.5 defensive stats per game. Juškaitė may not be the most exciting fantasy name out there, but at this point in the season, you’re probably not looking to hit a home run on the waiver wire. Juškaitė is currently rostered in just over 21 percent of ESPN leagues; that number is rising quickly, however, so make sure she isn’t a free agent in your league. Jade Melbourne is stepping up in Seattle The Seattle Storm are another team that are probably thinking more about draft lottery odds than winning basketball games. They’ve also been eliminated from playoff contention, and have no more reason to push their veterans (or injured players) than the Tempo do. One such veteran is guard Natisha Hiedeman, who was having a career year before she injured her shoulder last week. Through 36 games, Hiedeman is averaging 15.4 points, 1.9 3-pointers, 4.8 assists and 1.2 defensive stats, good for 27.2 fantasy points per game in standard leagues. With their most ball-dominant guard now on the bench until further notice, the Storm have given Melbourne a bigger role. She’s been modestly productive this season, averaging 9.3 points, 3.9 assists and 1.1 defensive stats, and she’s started 28 of the 36 games she’s played in. These aren’t, of course, eye-popping numbers, but Melbourne was significantly more productive in the Storm’s first game without Hiedeman, racking up 11 points, five rebounds and six assists in 35 minutes. It’s the playing time that’s most encouraging here; Seattle’s future may hinge on the development of frontcourt players Dominique Malonga and Awa Fam, but Melbourne is still young enough to be considered a potential part of that core if the Storm believe in her. Expect them to give her more reps alongside rookie Flau’jae Johnson until Hiedeman returns. Nia Coffey is hanging onto fantasy relevance—for now Last month, we discussed how Napheesa Collier’s return from ankle surgery would affect the rest of Minnesota’s rotation, and predicted that Coffey would take the biggest hit. That ended up being true: In 10 games with Collier in the lineup, Coffey averaged just 3.5 points, 2.6 rebounds and 0.8 defensive stats in just 13.9 minutes per game, all as a reserve. Though Coffey was one of the season’s most pleasant surprises through late June, it’s now obvious the Lynx saw her as more of a placeholder while their star forward got healthy. There’s one wrinkle here, though, and it’s an important one: The Lynx are now resting Collier. This isn’t much of a surprise, given how far ahead the Lynx are of the rest of the pack (and how things ended prematurely for them last season, partly due to Collier’s initial foot injury), and Coffey was there to pick up the slack. Last Friday, she got the start and played 30 minutes, racking up eight points, two 3-pointers and four defensive stats. This is something to keep a keen eye on for the rest of the regular season. We’ve seen how valuable of a fantasy player Coffey can be when she’s playing starters’ minutes. She was averaging 7.7 points, 5.3 rebounds, 1.5 3-pointers and 2.4 defensive stats before Collier returned to the lineup. The key will be knowing exactly when she’ll draw that assignment again. Collier was announced out due to rest over 24 hours before last Friday’s game, which gave fantasy managers plenty of time to put her on an IL spot and pick up someone else. Even if she’s not on your team, watch for similar news as the season winds down, and be ready to add Coffey, even if it’s just for a game.

articles.title: WNBA gameday discussion: Are the Dallas Wings the preferred first-round playoff opponent for all the top seeds?
articles.summary: For awhile now, the eight-team field for the 2026 WNBA playoffs has been unofficially set. articles._body: Gabby Williams and Kaitlyn Chen defend Paige Bueckers. | NBAE via Getty Images For awhile now, the eight-team field for the 2026 WNBA playoffs has been unofficially set. A post-All-Star slide by the Dallas Wings, with seven losses in nine games, combined with the persistence and pluckiness of the Portland Fire, however, did (slightly) open the door for Portland to replace Dallas in the top eight. With two wins in a row, the Wings have stabilized, giving them the opportunity to officially book their playoff bid over those visiting Fire on Tuesday evening (8 p.m. ET, NBA TV). On Sunday, both the New York Liberty and Washington Mystics secured their playoff fates. The Mystics’ win over the Fire, which required a 14-point comeback and career-high 31 points from Shakira Austin, sent the Liberty into the playoffs; their Saturday night escape against the Indiana put them into position for the passive clinching. The Fever’s win over the Sky then officially extinguished Chicago’s postseason chances and guaranteed the Mystics a spot in the playoffs. If Dallas gets the job done on Tuesday, all the pre-playoff drama will be contained to shifts up and down the top eight, and how such shakeups will determine first-round matchups. While the Minnesota Lynx have a firm hold on the No. 1 overall seed, with a four-game lead despite Monday night’s loss to the Golden State Valkyries, every other team’s fate can change, and possibly significantly, between now and the end of the regular season. Presuming the Wings are in, the current first-round pairings would be: No. 1-seed Minnesota Lynx vs. No. 8-seed Dallas Wings No. 2-seed Golden State Valkyries vs. No. 7-seed Washington Mystics No. 3-seed Las Vegas Aces vs. No. 6-seed New York Liberty No. 4-seed Atlanta Dream vs. No. 5-seed Indiana Fever Which teams should be happy with this set up? Which teams should be angling for a different first-round foe? And which opponent should certain teams strive to avoid at all costs? Today, let’s take a quick look at the most likely matchup preferences for the current top-four seeds. Tomorrow, we’ll finish out the playoff field. No. 1-seed Minnesota Lynx (31-8) As the No. 1 seed with just eight losses on the season, and with two certified superstars capable of MVP-caliber play in Napheesa Collier and Olivia Miles, the Lynx should fear no first-round opponent. However, they would likely prefer to see the Wings stick into the No. 8 seed, rather than have them leap the Mystics and send DC into the No. 8 spot. While Minnesota has dominated Dallas, sweeping the season series 4-0 with ease, they’ve best tested by Washington, with the Mystics even taking a game off the Lynx in Target Center. Size and physicality, especially on the glass, stand as the Lynx’s biggest weaknesses, and those areas, in contrast, are where the Mystics thrive. Yet, last Friday night, the Lynx earn eda 2-1 season series-clinching win over the Mystics in DC, despite losing the rebounding battle and not having the services of Collier, who was out for rest. Minnesota’s superior shotmaking overcame Washington’s rebounding and free throw advantages. But if the shots fall short in the playoffs, things could get tricky for the Lynx in a Mystics matchup. No. 2-seed Golden State Valkyries (26-11) The Valkyries, as things currently stand, are slated to have to confront all the challenges that come with the Mystics’ size and physicality. Although they are responsible for holding the Mystics to an absolutely anemic 49-point outing in early July, the other two Golden State-Washington matchups, both held in San Francisco, were much more tightly-contested, with the fact that DC stole a game in Ballhalla confirming that Mystics are probably the most fearsome lower seed for any higher-seeded team. While the final game between the two teams will be played this Thursday, the Liberty, at least thus far, haven’t given the Valkyries too much trouble. With another win in Barclays, Golden State would enter a series against New York with confidence, despite the Liberty’s championship pedigree. Golden State’s best-in-the-league ability to induce poor shooting nights against opponents has particularly shined against New York. Yet, just like the Lynx, the Wings have to be the preferred opponent for the Valkyries. They swept the season series 3-0, flexing their defensive prowess by keeping Paige Bueckers in check in all three games. No. 3-seed Las Vegas Aces (26-13) The Aces, however, are the higher seed that do not want to see the Wings on the other side. Dallas won the first three of the four matchups between the two teams, lighting up Vegas for 90 or more points in all three victories. Considering it took a near-miracle for the Aces to get one win off the Indiana Fever, on top of the trouble they had putting away the injured Fever in last season’s second round, Vegas likely would prefer to avoid that matchup. They also probably wouldn’t be thrilled to see New York stick in the No. 6 seed. Despite their overall uninspiring season, the Liberty have performed particularly well against the Aces. But how much better would a first-round matchup with the Mystics be? Vegas did win the season series 2-1, recently notching two-straight home wins over DC. However, the Mystics, like the Liberty, have an excess of interior size to throw at A’ja Wilson. Conversely, Vegas has been quite comfortable against Golden State and Atlanta. An uneven Aces defense has succeeded in shutting down the Valkyries, and while the Dream finally defeated the Aces in their most-recent matchup, snapping Vegas’ streak of six-straight win, the Aces, and A’ja in particular, have owned Atlanta. No. 4-seed Atlanta Dream (25-13) So, we know Atlanta wants to avoid Vegas. Golden State should also be a no-go for Atlanta. articles.title: The Chicago Sky had no match for Kelsey Mitchell and Caitlin Clark, and now they’re eliminated from playoff contention
articles.summary: The final showdown between the Chicago Sky and Indiana Fever had one storyline after the next. For the Sky, capping off a home stand in which they won three straight. Sydney Taylor’s individual dominance despite being on a minutes restriction due to a groin injury. Natasha Cloud bringing the noise.
articles._body: Natasha Cloud defends Kelsey Mitchell. | NBAE via Getty Images The final showdown between the Chicago Sky and Indiana Fever had one storyline after the next. For the Sky, capping off a home stand in which they won three straight. Sydney Taylor’s individual dominance despite being on a minutes restriction due to a groin injury. Natasha Cloud bringing the noise. DiJonai Carrington’s return from the injured list. Plus, wanting to finish the season on a high note. For the Fever, it’s Caitlin Clark being Caitlin Clark. Aliyah Boston sidelined due to injury. Kelsey Mitchell in command. And Sophie Cunningham…no explanation needed. All those factors burst the doors at Wintrust Arena off the hinges Sunday night. The first half ended with the Sky leading 51-50. The pace on both sides was furious and neither was giving an inch. Cloud supercharged the offense by penetrating the paint and shooting from long range. Kamilla Cardoso was solid inside and on the boards. Aicha Coulibaly came off the bench to add additional strength and quickness at both ends. Q1 so far ➡️ #skytown pic.twitter.com/a6IQlE5iVy — Chicago Sky (@chicagosky) August 23, 2026 It seemed as if the Sky had a chance. Until the 3rd quarter. Mitchell and Clark lit up the Chicago skyline, hitting shot after shot as the Fever went on a 17-7 run that began at the close of the first half. However, the Sky clawed their way back towards the end of the quarter, and that was right when the intensity burst through seams. With 1:22 left in the quarter, Cloud hit an off-balance spin shot in the lane to bring the Sky within six, 81-75. Then, she traded barbs with former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom, who was sitting under the basket. Kanter, who recently announced he was “entering” the 2027 WNBA Draft as part of an anti-transgender athlete crusade, was kicked out of the game and received boos from the stands. Kanter was wearing a shirt that read “Woman (noun) an adult female.” The game resumed and Fever didn’t budge. They outscored the Sky 30-13 in the fourth quarter to secure a 113-90 win, eliminating the Sky from postseason contention. no better backcourt duo in the league 😈 Caitlin Clark and Kelsey Mitchell both dropped 30+ PTS in the same game for the THIRD time in their careers last night in Chicago. the most games by a duo in WNBA history. pic.twitter.com/ytlizo3kYd — Indiana Fever (@IndianaFever) August 24, 2026 Clark finished with 37 points, including eight 3-pointers. Mitchell came away with 30 points and six 3-pointers. Cloud led the Sky with 16 points and seven assists; she was 7-for-9 from the field. Azurá Stevens added 14 points and eight rebounds. Cardoso scored 11 points, grabbed six rebounds and was a perfect 7-for-7 from the foul line. Coulibaly added 12 points, as well as six boards. Carrington finished with seven points and three rebounds. Taylor finished with four points, going 0-for-9 from the 3-point line. Afterward, Stevens talked about the lessons learned from this home stretch as they prepare to hit the road, emphasizing: Not to get too down. We played two really great games. Tonight, we didn’t get it, but we have a couple road games coming up that we gotta regroup for and be ready for. So just not to take this one too hard. Before the game, head coach Tyler Marsh said Taylor was a “big boost” for them given her recent string of individual performances, including the buzzer-beater win against the Golden State Valkyries last Friday. Despite her struggles against the Fever, Marsh remained optimistic about Taylor, noting: I think we’ve gotten so used to Sydney just being Sydney that we don’t give her the grace of having a game like tonight, and it’s unfair to her. We’re gonna keep trying to find ways to give her the ball and she’s gonna win some more games for us. Cloud didn’t speak to the media about the incident with Kanter. According to Colin Salao of Front Office Sports , she met with the team and league security. Dispatch and latest updates from Chicago on the incident between Natasha Cloud and Enes Kanter Freedom: pic.twitter.com/yRBqAn6WRz — Colin Salao (@colincsalao) August 24, 2026 Marsh said to Salao, “We stand with Tash.” He also provided a message to Kanter and others through Alissa Hirsh of the Chicago Sun-Times , stating, “If you come to a game, you should probably come to enjoy the basketball, and that seems pretty simple to me. I think these players deserve that, and have earned that.“
